utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've been delayed, as I understand it, because building works at the Detention Unit have delayed the accused's arrival. We will sit until 2.00 to try and make up some of the time. We'll take the normal breaks at the normal times. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I recollect well that we discussed in public session the fact that the Defence Minister of Serbia, General Simovic, had appointed, or rather, given the proposal for the commander of the Krajina TO, General Djujic? I think this was in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, allow me to put a question without mentioning the witness's name, keeping my promise not to make any such omissions regarding protective measures. I hope you will be able to have this translated. I have been given a statement by fax in handwriting, signed precisely by Lieutenant Colonel General (retired) Ilija Djujic. I will not read it out in extenso. Anyway, it's hard to read his handwriting. But he does say: "During one of my visits to Knin, I was visited in my native house by C-061." He lists his positions, the positions he held, and then he said: "In that family home of mine, C-061 asked me to accept the duty of commander of SAO Krajina and to form the defensive structure," et cetera, et cetera. I am giving you this statement which clearly shows that this would-be witness is not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a question for him. It's not a question about the statement. It's his evidence. Now, what's alleged, Milan Babic, you've heard what's been read out, it's alleged by this person that Djujic visited you, and you asked him to accept the duty of the commander and form a defensive structure. Did anything like that happen at all?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I correct you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I have read out, it was not the general, General Djujic, who visited the witness but the witness visited General Djujic in his family home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he went to see him to ask him what he asked him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following is true: I did know General Djujic even before the appointment, and I would meet with him. Among other things, I did visit the house that he was rebuilding in his native village. He also came to visit me in my office, but the appointment of General Djujic as commander of the TO of SAO Krajina occurred in the way I have described.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, for the reasons which have been explained before when you've produced statements or documents from persons outside the courtroom. The only way to get that sort of evidence in is to call the witness himself. It's not evidence; it's merely his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us clear up one further point before I continue with the questions where I left off yesterday. You said yesterday that you knew nothing about the money collected in the diaspora, amounting 169.417 dollars, and that that was not handed to you. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I never received such a quantity of money in cash myself. There were situations when people from the diaspora would contact the Serbian radio-television through me or in some other ways, and in that way conveying the money, but I absolutely do not remember personally receiving such a sum of money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please comment, then, on this very brief note. It is a note written by the Minister of Finance of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and signed by him, Ratko Veselinovic. It is his note in which he says: "At the end of 1994, the Ministry of Finance --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I will not read out the name, but you will be able to gather yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "-- to Ratko Veselinovic, a list of our citizens from the diaspora was handed in, people who had collected funds and who wanted to help their people. When handing over this list, the request was made to check whether these funds were deposited in the budget of the Republic of Serbia Krajina or the municipality budget. As these funds were handed in to --" and then the position and name of M. Babic is given -- "amounting to 169.417 US dollars, having made checks through the foreign exchange inspector, the Finance Minister established that no such funds were invested into the budget of the Republic of Serbian Krajina or into the budget of the Municipal Assembly of Knin. "In the foreign exchange inspectorate, proceedings were instituted against --" the name of C-061 is given -- "but in view of the fact that he held the position which he did --" and then that position is defined -- "the proceedings were conducted in secrecy. The proceedings were instituted by the foreign exchange inspectorate, and in charge was Vladimir Velebit who was killed in the Serbian Krajina under mysterious circumstances and that is why this note is being made. Signed Ratko Veselinovic, Minister of Finance of the Republic of Serbian Krajina." As this is no statement of a witness but, rather, a note drafted in connection with the event I have just described, I assume that at least this can be accepted into evidence. If not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. What is the date of the note, please? Has it got a date on it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am afraid I don't have -- there is no date on this, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see the document. While that's being collected, perhaps we could be reminded of the exhibit number for the collection, which in the end was exhibited, I think. It's the list. Yes, D63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We note that this has a fax date on, it's pointed out by the registry, of December 1999. It's got another one on of more recent date, November this year. But in any event, we will admit it subject to the right of the Prosecution to make any objections in due course. Perhaps the Prosecution could see it now. Perhaps we could have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Defence Exhibit 64, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And perhaps the witness should see it before he comments on it. If you'd just have a look at that, M. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honours, while the witness is reading it, the Prosecution would object against the admissibility of this document, because what it amounts to is actually a statement of a person signing this document, explaining something that happened years ago, and it's actually a written statement about facts of that time, and it's given in 1999, and as we also saw, that same date was on the fax list. The fax list had that same date, and it's actually a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Since we don't have it translated, it's difficult for us to judge. What we'll do is we will admit it but subject to oral argument in due course when we have a translation. Yes, M. Babic. Do you want to make any comment on that document now you've had the chance to read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about this. I said that I only recollect that some funds were handed over in my apartment to the director of Serbian radio television. I don't exactly remember the sum involved. As for this, I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does it represent the truth, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is written here, no. I do not remember that, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Let the document be handed back, unless you want to ask any more questions about it, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read out the whole document, and I think it contains sufficient information. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just didn't understand the answer that you gave that the money was handed over in your apartment, the money from the diaspora, in your apartment, to the director of television. Which television?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not this money that I'm referring to but a certain sum of -- for the Serbian radio television in Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of that director of the Serbian television in Knin to whom the money was given?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lazar Macura.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So Lazar Macura, in your apartment, received some money but not this sum that is mentioned in this note.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On another occasion, not in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that first occasion if this was another occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He received a donation for the Serbian radio and television. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're claiming that you never received money from Serbs in the diaspora intended for aid to the people of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did receive 10.000 dollars from a man called Prica in the presence of Rasuo, and Caslav Ocic gave me 5.000 American dollars from Momcilo Djujic, he said, and asked me to sign a note of thanks, and I gave this money to Rasuo and the representative offices in Belgrade. I received support from the diaspora for the elections, for my party, amounting to about 7.000, I think it was Canadian dollars, so -- and I also received from certain people --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Caslav Ocic at that time, at the time when the Vance Plan was under consideration?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Caslav Ocic was the Minister of Foreign Affairs in the government of Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember his article in the newspaper in which he wrote that Cyrus Vance had bribed me with $120 million to accept the Vance Plan? Do you perhaps recollect that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This is just one of the minor details that I was accused of in those days. But let us move on with regard to the events that, as we have seen, you know very little about, especially in 1990. Did you know anything about the illegal arming of paramilitary formations in Croatia, in the first place the members of the HDZ and all the other formations that I listed yesterday, so I don't have to repeat them today, all their different names.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew as much as was broadcast by the media, and in the spot or announcement of the information service of the federal Secretariat of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that already on the 11th of November, 1990, the Presidency of Yugoslavia, at a session it held, was informed of a channel for illegal import of weapons to Croatia as early as the 11th of November, 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had heard through the media reports by the Secretariat for National Defence on the illegal arming of the HDZ and other people who were not part of the legal police structure of the government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, since at that meeting of the Presidency of the SFRY, Stipe Mesic, as a member of the Presidency, was present as well as Ante Markovic as the president of the federal executive council, that through them, the leadership of Croatia was immediately informed that this illegal channel had been unveiled, discovered, and then Spegelj got the message, "Flee abroad, otherwise, you'll be arrested." Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about these events in connection with the Presidency. What I do know about those events, I just said how I learnt about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, is the following correct -- I'm just going to ask you whether it's true or not and you can give a yes or no answer. You don't have to talk about matters that I'm not asking you about. Is it true that after the -- before the general attack on the -- by the Croatian paramilitary formations on the JNA units, the new HDZ authorities in Croatia had quite a number of clashes and conflicts with the Serb people in Krajina? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was some sort of order for a complete blockade of the barracks by Croatia, and before that, there were conflicts and clashes between the military formations or, rather, the police forces and the DB forces, state security on the one side, and the Croatian police on the other side. So the DB from Krajina on one side and the police on the other, the Croatian police force. Those clashes took place before that, before the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: Did the first clash take place, regardless of the fact that you don't seem to remember anything from 1990, but did it take place on the 17th of August, 1990, in Kninska Krajina when the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Croatia demanded that the police station in Knin be renamed and called by a different way, with a plaque up in front of the door, and instead of the Yugoslav flag, the Croatian flag should be put out with the chequerboard emblem and that the policemen that made up the police force in that station be replaced by Croatian policemen? Did this first clash take place on the 17th of August, then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 17th of August but two or three days later, I think. And the clash did not take place in Knin either, and it wasn't a real clash, actually. Or, rather, there was a conflict when the special police force of the Croatian government in Split started out towards Knin and when some people were armed at the barricades in Civljani and they shot, they started firing. The police went back to Vrlika and that was the incident in question. The next incident that occurred, after the 17th of August, that is to say, round about that time, according to the information that I had received from policemen in Drnis is when Ante Bujas, the chief of the police from Sibenik issued an order, having received instructions from the Internal Affairs Ministry, to disarm the barricades at Klanac between Tepljuh and the other Kosovo area, and that the special police units from Drnis should move towards Knin, whereas the policemen from Knin, the Serbs and Croats, refused to carry out the order and it was never actually implemented. So that's what happened in Knin in the month of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me remind you: The commander of the police station at that time in Knin, was that Milan Martic? Was he the commander who, with 19 other policemen, referred back to Petar Gracanin, the Internal Affairs Minister, to ask him to stop this violence over the police station in Knin? And as the federal secretariat didn't take any steps to do that, he had to fend for himself and do the best he could. Was that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander, or komandir, was a man by the name of Vujko. He was a Serb by origin from around Skradin and previously he had served in the Serb police force. And there was a letter which was drafted on the 5th of July, I think it was. It was published in the Politika newspaper, and it was signed by most of the policemen in Knin, and this was to organise a petition with all the signatures. This was organised in fact, this petition, by Martic, Nikola Manovic, Zelenbaba, and some others - I can't remember their names - and most of the policemen of the Knin police station. They wrote this letter to Petar Gracanin, saying that they refused to have the new uniforms and insignia prescribed by the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia. Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, then, what was Martic then at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic was an inspector in the police station in Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, then: This conflict, clash, when the new Croatian authorities took this step and the clash was a reaction to this on the part of the policemen in Knin, they reacted by sending a petition to the federal Minister of Internal Affairs. Is that right? Is that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they had organised the signing of a petition, and this petition or letter was printed in the Politika newspaper at the beginning of July, and they did not wish to have the police force -- the name of the police force in Knin changed to Redarstvo, they did not accept the new caps with the new insignia and emblems of Croatia, and the uniforms that were prescribed, and they were supposed to be black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the reasons why they refused to accept the chequerboard emblem and those black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until then, the insignias they wore, worn by the policemen in the Socialist Republic of Croatia, was the five-pointed star. The Ministry of the Interior or, rather, the Croatian government, even before the changes that were made to the constitution of Croatia, stipulated that the police should wear the insignia and emblems of the so-called chequerboard which was the old Croatian emblem, the chequerboard emblem. And there were proposals, whether this was formally done or not, at the level of the Croatian government that the name for the police force be the Redarstvo or "Orderly" and later on, the police of Croatia. Now, whether for some time this term, which was Redarstvo, whether it was ever used officially I don't know, but in the common parlance, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why were these people so sensitive to the "sahovic" or the chequerboard coat of arms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Socialist Republic of Croatia's coat of arms was the chequerboard emblem, the old Croatian coat of arms, but it was reduced slightly, it was a little smaller. So the emblems of corn, sea, and so on with the five-pointed star was what they wanted to abolish, and introduce the chequerboard coat of arms and emblems without any of the additional symbols. So this was the old Croatian coat of arms. And this was commented by most of the Serbs in Croatia at that time, the political parties as well as the Serbs in the police force in Knin, as symbols which bring to mind the NDH, the Independent State of Croatia during the war. Although I listened to Mr. Seks, he explained this, whether cynically or not, but he said that the Ustasha chequerboard began with a white field in the upper row whereas this one now the new chequerboard coat of arms began with the red field, the red square. But this was not really taken seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what about the reactions? Did the people react because these were in fact Ustasha symbols?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation was that they brought to mind and resembled the Ustasha emblems and that it associated people with the Independent State of Croatia, the Ustasha state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have any understanding for that or did it remind you of that as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were opposed to a unilateral step of this kind, that is to say that the majority in the Croatian parliament should impose such emblems as state emblems and coats of arms, that is to say the official coat of arms of the Republic of Croatia. We wanted this to be discussed with the representatives of the Serbs living in Croatia, which means that we were opposed to having symbols of this kind introduced without the acquiescence of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I didn't ask you that. What I was asking you was did you personally consider this to be Ustasha symbols?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was laying too great an emphasis on the Ustasha Croatian emblems, because the Ustasha chequerboards in fact had the letter 'U' added to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take it, then, that you did not consider that they were Ustasha symbols?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was suggested in a way. It sort of associated us with the Independent State of Croatia, and by overemphasising Croatian national symbols, this did resemble and bring to mind the former symbols although these weren't the Ustasha symbols in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you consider that it was not an Ustasha symbol?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not associate me with those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that you were not reminded of the Ustasha symbols? Is that what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our public debates, we called them pro-Ustasha symbols. I can't remember exactly what we called them, but not as an exclusive Ustasha symbol. That's what I considered. Although they did sort of resemble them and remind us of them and so perhaps the word was actually used. I can't quite remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your answer is perhaps but you can't remember exactly. Let's move on so as not to go on with this question for too long. Do you remember that the MUP of Croatia decided to have an airborne helicopter unit land at Knin and have ground forces from Sibenik, Split and Gospic move on the police station to take control of it, and this operation was led by the Deputy Minister of the Internal Affairs, Perica Juric, who returned to the country as a well-known Ustasha emigre, which he had been up until then, but the operative centre of the RV PVO reacted to prevent bloodshed. The air force and anti-aircraft units wanted to prevent the bloodshed by sending in the forces and thus thwarted the conflict that could have taken place between the police, the Croatian police on the one hand and the Knin police force on the other. Is that correct? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already spoken about what I know of those events that took Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. place on the 17th of August, 1990, in Knin, and the intimation that Croatian transporters were to arrive in Knin. Later on, I heard that Croatia had three, the Croatian air force had three APCs. One of them had broken down in Kosovo whereas another one was really stopped at Korenica in the Lika region. Later on, I learnt about the helicopters, that the helicopters had started out but that the JNA had prevented them from actually landing in Knin and they had to return back to Zagreb. Colonel Bajic later on explained this over television. He was the commander of the air force unit in Zagreb, Colonel Bajic was his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. The transcript, line 23, page 13, has attributed an answer of the witness to me. No doubt that will be corrected. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. To sum up, the police in those beginnings had clashes with the Serbs in Krajina, the newly established Croatian authorities, and the army acted to stop the conflicts and did not take anybody's side. All it did was to prevent the conflict; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that the army had indeed prevented the Croatian police from intervening in Knin, which means taking over the police station and preventing the referendum. So the army made it possible for the police station in Knin to remain independent of the control of the Croatian authorities and that the Serb referendum should go forward without impediment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that it was the message of the MUP to -- MUP of Croatia to all the other regional MUPs to ensure constant supervision of the garrison and for them to be on the ready to act if the orders came? Do you know of that order on the part of the Croatian police force?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the MUP of Croatia, on the 7th of December, 1990, issued orders for the activation of 50 per cent of the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly when this order was pronounced I don't know, but I did know myself that the Croatian MUP did increase its reserve formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that in the course of 1990, that is to say before any clashes ever took place which could be denoted as such, that over 70 cases were registered of provocation and physical attacks on members of the JNA in Croatia, individual ones, different ones?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of that particular figure. I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know about those attacks that took place in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All this was going on in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were clashes between the Croatian police and citizens in Petrinja who had fled to the Petrinja garrison and there were some clashes around that garrison. Now, what actually happened, I don't know. Whether it was between the police and army, I don't think it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you know nothing about the attacks, not only those by the police but the armed groups of civilians, the extremists, on members of the army, members of the JNA in 1990? You know nothing about that you say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for 1990, I don't remember. Whether I knew anything, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say you don't know. Now, do you know that the Presidency of the SFRY on the 9th of January, 1991, that is to say at the very beginning of the year, issued an order to disband all armed units which were not within the composition of the united armed forces of the SFRY and that this was to have been completed by the 19th of January, that is to say, within a space of ten days?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the Yugoslav state Presidency, because of the situation it found itself in, decided at a meeting of the 25th of January to call the president of the federal government and the federal Secretariat for National Defence and that an agreement was reached by which the -- by the 6th of January the reserve force was to be demobilised, of the police force in Croatia, and the units of the JNA be reduced to the peacetime level of readiness. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that the Presidency of the SFRY, at the insistence of the government of Croatia, extended the time limit, the deadline that it set for the 9th of January, it put it off for 48 hours because they explained that they were not able to implement the order in such a short space of time? So they asked for two more days, and the Presidency did indeed extend the deadline. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that on the 22nd of January, the Yugoslav state Presidency took note of the fact that disarmament had not taken place in Croatia and that Croatia was in fact arming itself and that a mobilisation was going on, quite the contrary to what had been agreed upon and promised in order to thwart and prevent the conflicts and for political issues to be settled by political means? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember one specific event that took place at that time when this disbanding was supposed to take place? The leadership of Croatia in fact handed out weapons in Osijek, and between the 19th and 20th of January, 1991, a driver Zdravko Tomsic [phoen] was seized with a supply of arms, and in Eastern Slavonia a similar incident took place, Darda. Do you remember these incidents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that. I heard that the police was handing out weapons to the reservists, and it was rumoured that their weapons were being handed out to the members of the HDZ. Now, I don't remember that specific case with the truck, that you mentioned, and the driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember that on the 5th of May, the Croatian paramilitary units blocked the barracks in Osijek and Gospic and that on the 8th of July, this was followed by an attack on JNA units which were providing security for the 25th of May bridge across the Danube River, Bracka Palanka? Do you remember those occurrences?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These incidents, which means the intensive blocking of the barracks, this wave started after the beginning of May, after the incident in Borovo Selo and Plitvice Lakes, Polaca, Benkovac, between Polaca and Kijevo, near Knin. And other events, the ones in Split, for example. So that was the time that we saw an escalation in the conflict and the protests that were going on, both on the part of Croatian citizens and the beginning of the blockade of the barracks, JNA barracks, and the blockades by members of the police, the guards, and who knows who else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the clash between the police that occurred in Pakrac in early March 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked you about this conflict. I asked you what was going on there, and you said everything would be all right and I could go to Knin. Later on, I read in the press that there had been a conflict between Serb citizens and the Croatian police, that the JNA had intervened, and the press even said that people had been killed. I think --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you know nothing about these events apart from what you read in the papers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I heard from the media, that something was going on there, then I called you on the phone. I was in Belgrade at the time. I rang you up. And then I read in the press about these events, and later on there was talk about them. But my knowledge of these events is not direct, it's indirect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, when you arrived there - in Knin, I mean, when you returned - did you find out whether this was correct, that over 600 policemen from the training centre in Lucko near Zagreb were on their way to Pakrac in three columns?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course we knew all about that. We were informed of that, but not directly. We did not have direct communication with Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the JNA intervene in time there with the same aim that they had in Knin to prevent inter-ethnic clashes and bloodshed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the conflict broke out there exactly, but later on I heard or read somewhere that Borisav Jovic had said that he had ordered an intervention by the JNA, and after that, he asked for the approval of the Presidency for the way in which the JNA became active in Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that a small unit was sent which prevented a clash and that, later on, teams arrived from the federal Ministry of the Interior to solve the problems that had occurred in Pakrac, to prevent serious consequences?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the intervention but not about the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I assume you know that although everything was done to prevent the conflict that was imminent, that it did take place. It did break out, not only between representatives of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior and the Serbian citizens living in these areas but that also fire was opened from one of these armoured personnel carriers belonging to the Croatian police which I mentioned and which fired on JNA soldiers stationed in front of the Pakrac hospital. Are you aware of this event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I'm not aware of the details of what happened in Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Do you know that within the scope of these same efforts and in this same -- in this same context, on the 30th of March, 1991, the Plitvice Lakes were taken by force, on which occasion two men were killed and 20 wounded? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had personal knowledge of these events in the afternoon of that day. I think it was the last day of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intervention of the special police of Croatia took place after forces were deployed, forces of the Krajina police, and I don't know who else Martic deployed there. A police station was to be opened in Plitvice, but the Serb forces deployed by Martic were instead deployed in battle formation. After that, the Croatian police intervened, and the first clash occurred, as I heard, behind the bridge over the river Korana at the entrance to Plitvice. The Serbian forces fired a -- fired a rifle grenade, which missed its mark, and then the clash broke out, and a Croatian policeman was killed. I don't know if it was then or a little later, the Serbs retreated from the bridge. Then there was a skirmish. Rifle shots were fired and a Serb was killed in the area of the hotel in Plitvice. And the result of all this was that the Croatian police took over the national park area as far as the hotel or, rather, the memorial home of the 6th Lika Division near Mukinje. The JNA intervened from the north in the direction of Plitvice, and they deployed themselves in the area of Mukinje. I met General Stimac personally who was in charge of this JNA intervention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the purpose of this intervention? Was it to separate the warring sides? Is this correct or not? Was it not to create a buffer zone between the two hostile parties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army separated the Krajina police, which was under the control of the Serbian DB, and the special police of Croatia, which had taken the area of the hotel. So the army was actually deployed as a buffer in the Mukinje area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the army was serving was a buffer. Who was there from the Serbian DB controlling the Krajina police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Before the intervention, before the effort to set up a Krajina SUP police station in Plitvice, there was a man whose name I can't remember now, although I know him, and he knew what was going on. I can't say exactly whether it was he who intervened for Martic to deploy his forces in battle formation rather than trying to set up a police station, but the DB structure did have an influence in this particular instance. The man from the DB of Serbia had all the information, and I suspect that it was he who intervened with Martic and got him to deploy his forces in battle formation rather than simply trying to set up a police station. That is what I know about the functioning of this structure after April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I can understand, you're constantly drawing conclusions but you have no facts to present. You're simply drawing conclusions on the basis of your assumptions or on the basis of a goal that is to be reached. This is the first time I'm hearing that the DB of Serbia participated in the clash on Plitvice between the forces of the Krajina and the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was well aware of the situation. I don't know what the extent of his influence was, but I do know that instead of opening a police station, Martic deployed his forces in battle formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That explains nothing. Tell me, is it correct that on the 31st of March, Croatian policemen, as they were called at the time, arrived as guests in the national park of Plitvice? They were posing as visitors, and they attempted to ambush the police of Krajina from within.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was talk of this, that some were in there, but I have described the events as I learned about them at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Croatian policemen came disguised as visitors in order to attack from the inside, and the DB of Serbia knew about this and organised, I can conclude from what you're saying, they influenced the police of the Krajina to organise themselves. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have described very precisely what I know about the outbreak of the clash. And as for the members of the Croatian police in civilian clothes, there was talk of this but I know nothing specific about it. As for the influence of the DB of Serbia, as I said, that was my conclusion. The facts are what I said. I have told you what I heard at the time had happened. And in the afternoon, I arrived there; from then on, I was in Korenica and I was able to find out for myself what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one second. Mr. Witness, could you tell us the difference between deploying the forces in battle formations and the setting up a police station in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you're setting up a police station, you have to find a building, you have to put offices in there, the chief of police, criminal inspector, a traffic policeman, administrative staff, and the administrative structure should be put in place as is usually in a police station. Battle formation is something different. No police station was opened. Men who were armed, in uniform and not in uniform, were deployed over an area of several kilometres in the area of the national park, and they were deployed on the edges of the national park facing the territory controlled by the Croatian government. That's what the difference is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you have spent quite some time in The Hague now, the policemen you see around here, are they sitting in a police station or are they on the beat? Are they walking the streets and controlling -- or patrolling the area of their responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a proper question. It's not for the witness to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you are constantly mentioning the DB, do you remember that to my question when I asked you to enumerate some names, you managed to enumerate three, and that was a mistake. You mentioned the wife of one of the people involved who was from the area, and probably she came to visit her parents, accompanied by her husband, and she was not on some sort of secret mission. So this influence of the DB of Serbia amounted to occasional visits, private or official, it doesn't matter, by only three persons, so why can't you enumerate at least ten?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I enumerated the chiefs of the DB who were in the Krajina and the chiefs who were in Belgrade. As for the operatives in the field and the agents, I didn't know about these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all these chiefs were from the DB of Krajina. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic was not from the DB of the Krajina. He was your chief policeman, your associate. You were his immediate superior. His office, up to the summer, was in the old MUP building. He was close to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If he was in Belgrade, how could he have been in Knin? I understood that you had had lunch with him and his wife. I assume that he had gone with his wife to visit her parents in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't lunch; we had coffee in the Seher restaurant in Belgrade, in the Venjak [phoen] area, in the garden of the restaurant, in fact, and he called me over to introduce his wife to me and to have a chat with me. He wanted to establish friendly relations with me. And after your intervention and after you criticised the fact that I had had to call you for Frenki to be withdrawn from the Krajina, that was the reason he wanted to chat with me, and that was in August in Belgrade, in August 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it correct that in early May, on the eve of the referendum in Croatia, the Serbian referendum in Croatia, the Croatian police caused several incidents and that there was an incident in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, I heard about the clash in Borovo Selo from Vojislav Seselj first. He had been in Knin and he told me that two of his men had been killed in Borovo Selo. Later on, I heard from Frenki that his men, that means the DB, had used an anti-aircraft gun to fire on the Croatian police in Borovo Selo. Later on, I heard that the commander, the local commander of the defence of Borovo Selo was -- his name was Vukasin Soskocanin, and for reasons that were never explained, he drowned in the river Danube. Later on, I heard many stories on the Croatian side as to how this clash had occurred: That the Croatian police had set out for Borovo Selo and that there had been resistance to their entry into Borovo Selo and that a large number of men had been killed. The Croatian police had many men killed, and this caused enormous indignation in Croatia. There were funerals of policemen going on for days and days. This was on television, and public opinion in Croatia became very hostile after this event toward Serbia and toward the Serbs and also toward Yugoslavia, towards everything that, in their view, posed a threat to Croatia. On the 2nd of May, as I said, Vojislav Seselj --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's be brief. Let's cut this short, if we may. You have described the event exactly as it was presented by the Croatian press and Croatian propaganda, the propaganda of the time, and that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this event first from Vojislav Seselj, later from Franko Simatovic, and later on from people from Borovo, and also I saw what the Croatian media were reporting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is my information correct that the Serbs from Borovo Selo, as a gesture of goodwill in negotiations with the police, had said they would remove the barricades and that they would normalise the situation because they had been promised that no one would be attacked, arrested, or taken away, would go missing, and that they had removed the barricades, that the police had arrived in the village at the agreed time but with two buses, with two terrain vehicles and one passenger vehicle full of policemen, and instead of talking to the population about normalising the situation, they opened fire on all sides and that's how the clash occurred. Is this a correct description of the events in Borovo Selo or what you have just explained, which is the version put forward by the Croatian propaganda at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from people from Borovo Selo that the Croatian police had arrived in buses. They even laughed because the Croatian police had been so stupid. They were not prepared for battle, they were simply sitting in buses, and they were allowed to enter into the village. They showed me the spot up to which they had allowed them to enter, and then they opened fire on them. That's what people, local people, actually told me. I don't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Those two buses full of policemen, two terrain vehicles and a passenger vehicle, so five vehicles full of policemen, two of which were buses, were attacked by the locals of Borovo Selo just like that, out of the blue. And what did those busloads of policemen armed to the teeth, what were they looking for in that village? So Borovo Selo attacked the police and not the police, fully armed, attacking the peasants in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Borovo Selo was not under the control of the Croatian police. What happened there before, I don't know. The Serbs had Borovo Selo under control and not the police. So that is how the conflicts arose. The Croatian police wanted to establish control over Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Borovo Selo, and they met with resistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, certainly resistance was put up. Borovo Selo didn't go to the police but the police, armed to the teeth, came to the village and opened fired on the village, on their houses, on the people, on the children, women, et cetera. Is it true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his account. He's given his account of what he's heard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what we can read in the Croatian press, what he has just told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the event in Borovo Selo on Easter, the 2nd of May, 1991 - it was Easter - that there were no JNA units there at the time and that the entire event occurred outside the area of responsibility of any JNA units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the JNA intervened after those events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did it intervene? Again to separate the clashing parties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, between the Serbian forces in Borovo Selo and the Croatian forces outside Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again, to act as a buffer and avoid continued conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It positioned itself between two conflicting parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you remember the announcement from the expanded session of the Presidency of the SFRY regarding four principles for resolving the political crisis in the country? The session was held on the 20th of August, 1991, and all members were present in addition to the members of the Presidency, as announced, that is why it was called an expanded session. Participating were the presidents of the republics or, rather, the presidents of the Presidencies of the republics, the president of the Assembly of Yugoslavia, the president of the federal government, or Prime Minister, the vice-president of the Assembly, the presidents of the federal chamber of the Assembly, the federal Secretary for Foreign Affairs, the Minister for Justice and Administration, the Minister for Development, the Deputy Minister for Defence, and that the session was chaired by the president of the Presidency of the SFRY, Stipe or Stjepan Mesic, the one who testified here and who is now president in Croatia but whereas he should really be in prison. Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that is when the principles were agreed on. So the Presidency in full composition, the presiding officer was that same Stjepan Mesic, and four principles were established. Do you know them? The first was respect of every people or nation to self-determination, including the right to secession and unification. Any change of external and internal borders is unacceptable by unilateral acts and use of force but only and exclusively if such changes do occur, then it must be on the basis of the right of peoples to self-determination and through a democratic procedure and by legal means. That was adopted at that session chaired by Stjepan Mesic, attended by the whole Presidency and all the top leaders of the Yugoslav state, which was in one -- still in one piece at the time. Secondly, respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Milosevic, we must have time for questions. You're supposed to be questioning him, not making speeches. Does that help you? Do you remember that, M. Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now and you can continue after the break. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, is there any dispute that the Yugoslav leadership in full composition gave top priority to things being resolved by peaceful means and on the basis of the right of peoples to self-determination in a democratic procedure and by legal means? Doesn't that disprove your explanations of the use of the right of peoples to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what is the actual question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just read out to you principle number 1, which says that on the basis of the right of peoples to self-determination in a democratic procedure and in a legal way, things needed to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two understandings of that principle of self-determination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking to you about understandings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish what he was going to say. You are putting things to him and then trying to force him into some sort of corner. He must be entitled to reply himself. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two understandings or interpretations of the realisation of that right. One was that that right is exercised within republics and through the republics. That was the concept upheld by Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia, Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the other was your position regarding the right of self-determination, which was that regardless of republican borders, the nations of Yugoslavia, the recognised nations, including the Serb nation, were entitled to decide which state they would live in regardless of republican borders. And through -- not only in their mother republic, that is Serbia, but in other republics too. In other words, that that right to self-determination can ignore the boundaries of republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that I read out to you that it was -- that any change of both external and internal boundaries was unacceptable by force of arms? So external boundaries, secession from Yugoslavia by unilateral acts was unacceptable. This is what was established by that same Presidency chaired by Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I was not familiar with the details of that session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even if you are not familiar with the details, I am reading you a document which can be easily verified. For example, the third principle says the principle of equality, which implies the equality of all options, refraining from imposing one's will on others, and use of force. Also the principle of legality, which is means that political agreements must be legally sanctioned and a legal procedure established for its implementation. And then you talk about some law of Jovic's. This is the position of the Presidency of the SFRY, which says that legal procedures of implementation have to be established of any political agreement which has to be legally sanctioned without coercion and in conformity with the constitution of Yugoslavia. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you how those principles were interpreted in those days; in two different ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those days, as far as I can see from this, these principles were interpreted in a uniform manner by representatives and presidents of all the republics and the entire Presidency of the then-SFRY. That is precisely why I'm quoting them to you, because that is in complete contradiction with what you are saying. But let us move on. Is there any dispute that SFRY existed as a sovereign state right up until the establishment of the FRY? That is the 27th of April, 1992, when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established. Before that, there was the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was your interpretation. But the international conference, and especially the so-called Badinter Commission of that conference, stated towards the end of autumn 1991 - I think it was in November, to be precise - that the SFRY was in the process of disintegration, and later on it was stated that it had collapsed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is quite a different matter. But even in the documents of this illegal prosecution, what I have said is written, that is, until the formation of the FRY, SFRY existed as a state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Croatia recognised by the United Nations on the 22nd of May, 1992? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is the correct date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by the European Union on the 15th of January, 1992, by many countries of the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Germany recognised Croatia, I think, on the 23rd of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The role of Germany, the Vatican, and other powers has been explained here. I'm asking you about recognition by the European Union. So it was on the 15th of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 8th of October, 1991, that the three-month moratorium expired regarding the independence of Croatia and Slovenia which was agreed upon at Brioni, and that after that term had expired, Croatia declared that it had become an independent state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us clear up this thing. Is there any dispute that throughout this period and after this recognition of Croatia, the territory of Krajina was a United Nations protected area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry; could you repeat the question? I can't read out the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Croatia was recognised on the 22nd of May, 1992, by the United Nations, and on the 15th of January by the European Union. Is it true that after that time and throughout, the territory of Krajina was a protected area by the United Nations, according to the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From February -- from the end of February 1992, the Security Council adopted a resolution deciding that four -- four areas should be formed under UN protection. So Krajina and parts of the territories of Slavonia which were not part of Slavonia and Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that all Security Council resolutions, including the one 740 of the 4th of February, 743 of the 21st of February, and 762 of the 30th of June, 1992, and 802 of the 25th of January, 1993, and the Vance Plan, as well as the report of the UN Secretary-General dated the 3rd of February, 1992; 15th of February, 1992; 17th of July, 1992; 10th of February, 1993, that they all speak about UN protected areas and about peacekeeping operations in Yugoslavia? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They speak about it, but the plan according to which that protection was to have been provided, was not complied with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether these documents refer to that or not.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The protection applied to a state of demilitarisation, a mixed police force, the return of displaced persons. That was what the protection related to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it beyond doubt - and please give me a yes or no answer - that Croatia did not enjoy sovereignty over those territories?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the conference on the former Yugoslavia stated that there could be no change of republican borders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again you're giving me an answer to a question I have not put to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Croatian laws did not apply to those territories. Croatia did not assert its authority in those areas, if that is your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is my question. I will now quote to you from a report of the Secretary-General to the Security Council on the 4th of February, 1992, on page 5.D, and I will quote the whole of it: "It follows from this that areas under UN protection as hitherto would not be subject to the laws and institutions of the Republic of Croatia in the transitional period up to a political settlement." That is what is stated in the report of the UN Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Secretary-General also stated that in the Security Council, and this was adopted in February 1992, upon which the peace forces were deployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it then clear, and I'm asking you because these false charges speak of some sort of Serbian occupation, is it possible to speak about Serbian occupation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible to speak about the occupation by Serbia. Serbs were living there and Serbia had de facto authority in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you insist on that, I will use some quotations from this report of the Secretary-General linked to the course of the negotiating process regarding the Vance Plan, and here is what is stated in that report. As you have been referring to Mark Goulding, Deputy Secretary-General, here is what is stated in the report. And I'm reading the report, report of the UN Secretary-General dated the 4th of February, 1992, and it refers to the Vance Plan: "In the course of my talks --" in the course of his talks in Belgrade, Mr. Goulding once again was given unconditional assurances by Mr. Branko Kostic, the vice-president of the SFRY; Mr. Borisav Jovic, the president of the State Committee for Cooperation with the UN Regarding Peacekeeping; General Blagoje Adzic, acting federal Secretary of Defence of Yugoslavia, and the Chief of Staff of the JNA, that they accept the plan and that they will fully cooperate in its implementation. The President of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, also reiterated his full acceptance of the plan. "Also in Belgrade, Goulding --" this was point 10 that I read out. Now point 11: "He met with Adzic, the leader of the Serbian community in the region of Eastern Slavonia, who had an objection, but it was removed when Goulding explained that in a future resolution, it would be emphasised that the presence of the peacekeeping forces does not preempt or prejudice the political negotiations. When this had been explained to him, Mr. Adzic confirmed his acceptance of the UN plan." Then mention is made of the visit with Mr. Veljko Dzakula in another area. In fact, that is Western Slavonia, under UN protection, and we know that and that is what is stated here, who also accepted the plan. Point 12 of this report of the Secretary-General says: "Mr. Milan Babic, the leader of the Serbian community in the third proposed UN protected area, with whom Mr. Goulding had a five-hour long talk in Knin on the 27th of January, declared that he and his colleagues in the government --" and here it says, "of the so-called Serbian Krajina" -- "cannot accept the UN plan. He expressed the view that stating in the plan that UN protected areas in Croatia were unacceptable because they prejudiced the political settlement. He believed that Goulding's proposal that this be resolved by a Security Council document does not provide sufficient security. He rejected demilitarisation," et cetera. Let me not continue reading because it is very lengthy. "Babic added that only his government can assume responsibility towards the Security Council on behalf of his community," which is correct. "Goulding refused to make any changes in the plan which had been adopted by the Security Council." And then I just wish to quote from point 13: "In Zagreb, President Franjo Tudjman and senior officers in his government also declared that they could not accept the fundamental aspect of the plan whereby they withdrew the complete and unconditional support of that plan expressed to my envoy, Mr. Cyrus Vance, on the 1st of January." As we can see, it was only Tudjman and one of the leaders, by their refusal, actually delayed the implementation of the Vance Plan and prolonged the agony. And Tudjman declared, and I quote: "After international recognition of his republic, there are no political issues left to be negotiated. Mr. Goulding declared that such withdrawal of support for the plan by Mr. Tudjman would mean depriving the plan of two of its central elements and would undermine the basis for its acceptance by others. However, even after many hours of talks, Mr. Goulding did not manage to overcome this new and unacceptable -- unexpected obstacle to the deployment of international peace forces." Therefore, we see that Tudjman's position is in accord with the position of one of the leaders of one of these UN protected areas. And now I'm asking you: Do you remember -- since Tudjman later on, under pressure, accepted the deployment of these forces, however, in the paragraph regarding his refusal, he says that Croatia has been recognised and that there are no reason for any further negotiations. My question now is: Do you remember that international mediators, including Lord Carrington who chaired the conference, assessed that recognition of Croatia had been premature and that this marked the death toll for the peace conference on Yugoslavia? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have time just for a moment. First of all, do you want that document exhibited, Mr. Milosevic, the report of the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you wish. I can give it to you. However, this is in Serbian. And it's generally distributed B23451, February 2nd, original English. The title is "Further report of the Secretary-General Pursuant to Resolution 721 of 1991." You can probably find it in your archives. But I can give you this copy too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to go on. We'll ask the Prosecution if they can produce for us a copy. They should have one in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- we couldn't find anything that we have. We only -- what we have is actually the other document that Mr. Milosevic talked about, that was the Presidency session of the 20th of August. This we would have. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us have, then, the accused's copy, and we'll exhibit it and get it translated if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit number for it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Defence Exhibit 65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, M. Babic, you can -- you've heard a very extensive document read out. It may be you should have a copy in front of you so you can comment on it, and if you wish, we could go in at any stage to private session if you wish to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can comment on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Go into private session. 10 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can say is this: I had talks with Mr. Goulding in Knin at the end of January 1992, and we discussed the Cyrus Vance Plan. So what it states in this report is correct in the way that Mr. Goulding presented it to the United Nations Secretary-General. I can also add to this that on the occasion, I informed Mr. Goulding in detail about our positions with regard to the proposal to modify the plan. I informed him quite exactly about the zones and areas inhabited by the Serbs which come under the territory of the RSK and were not provided for as being protected. And I also told him of the municipality's plan, and I showed the areas which were not incorporated in the protection plan. I also discussed with him the possibility of having the Territorial Defence, once the JNA had left, transformed into a regional police force with the weapons that were prescribed for a mixed police force. And I also pointed out my reservations with respect to the implementation of Croatian laws on Krajina territory, which he mentions in the report. So it was my impression after the talk, and Mr. Goulding did say this, that we could continue our discussions on the issue, and some of our remarks and criticisms should be supported, whereas others would probably not be acceptable. And after that meeting, I really did expect to have another meeting with him. However, what followed was the Yugoslav State Presidency meeting, the expanded one on the 31st of January - and we've already discussed that - and we were forced, I personally was forced to accept the plan in its entirety and unconditionally. They didn't even want to listen to any amendments to the plan. There was absolutely no discussion on that score, with respect to this document, that is. Now, I don't know if you want me to read out the whole report and then to make some more comments. It's rather a lengthy report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We've heard it read out. The part that we've read out, is there any comment you wish to make in that part which deals with you and your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point in time, I was president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and I represented the Serbian community in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, as we are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it clear that in this report by the Secretary-General about your talks with Mark Goulding, that what you claimed that you explained to Mark Goulding with respect to the acceptance of the plan is very much different to what he says and what is stated in the UN Secretary-General's report about the failure to accept the plan? And how come that it is only you and Tudjman at that particular time had the same position not to accept the plan, with different explanations? Each of you had your own explanations.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to what I said, I told you of the modifications I had sought. Mr. Goulding told me the issues that were debatable and others that were not. So we were not able to discuss the substance of the plan. There was no change to that, no substantial changes which would not make the plan a demilitarisation plan. So all we could discuss was the military formations or units to remain in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he states quite clearly what you discuss. I don't think we need to comment on that. But you go on to say afterwards that the Yugoslav side didn't adhere to the plan, or something along those lines. So I'm going to read out a very brief excerpt from the Resolution 802 of the 25th of January, 1993. It is the UN Security Council Resolution number 802 of the 25th of January, 1993. The Security Council, and this is the third line: "Deeply concerned." Before that it says: We confirm Resolution such-and-such and our attachment to the peace plan of the United Nations, the so-called Vance Plan, and then it goes on to state the number of the plan. And then the third line states as follows: "Deeply concerned about the information received from the UN Secretary-General on the 25th of January, 1993, with respect to the rapid and violent escalation and deterioration of the situation in Croatia which has arisen through the military attack by Croatian armed forces on -- in the area under the protection of the United Nations peacekeepers," and in brackets, "(UNPROFOR)." And then he goes on to call for unconditional changes to the peace plan of the United Nations. So as you can see, the Security Council expresses its deep concern because of the attack launched by Croatian armed forces in the UN protected area as early on as January 1993. So who was it who did not adhere to the plan, the Croatian side or the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither you nor Franjo Tudjman did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. There's no point in discussing something that is quite clearly set out in the documents. We needn't waste time in these polemics. You mentioned the Badinter Commission, and in the text of the Badinter Commission, which was highly prejudiced to the detriment of Yugoslavia, even there it is stated in the chapter on plan -- "United Nations Peace Plan for Yugoslavia," that was the heading of the chapter, and then underneath, it said "The Vance Plan" as a second heading, and point 1, it states: "The United Nations peace plan in Yugoslavia is to be a provisional arrangement for creating conditions for peace and security that are necessary for negotiations about an overall settlement to the Yugoslav crisis. This arrangement would not preempt the outcome of those negotiations." Is there anything to be challenged there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says in the plan itself, that it is a security operation, this demilitarisation, which does not preempt a political settlement. So it was the plan for demilitarisation and not a political plan. That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As we're still in private session, I should just like to refer to one more report by the UN Secretary-General, dated the 15th of February, 1992, and the title is "Further report of the United Nations Secretary-General pursuant to UN Security Council Resolution 721 of 1991," which reflects in fact what I said all along, that is to say, your persistent refusal to accept the plan. And in point 7 with respect to Krajina, this is what is stated: "I have received a letter dated the 11th of February from Borisav Jovic, president of the state committee which was set up in Belgrade for cooperation with the United Nations with respect to peace and the preservation of peace." And in his letter which is attached as an addendum along with the annex, Annex 4 of this report, Mr. Jovic describes the meeting of the Krajina Assembly at which 81 deputies voted in favour of the United Nations plan, nobody voted against, and there were six abstentions. "On the basis of the voting and the measures that were undertaken in this regard by a number of leaders from the area, Mr. Jovic states that the decision means a definitive and unconditional acceptance of the United Nations plan and full agreement to cooperation towards its implementation and recommends that I propose to the UN Security Council the deployment of the UN peacekeepers themselves." And point 8 says: "Mr. Jovic expressed the view that resistance to the plan on the part of one Serbian leader in the area, Mr. Milan Babic, does not have," in inverted commas, "any great importance. The members of the council must know that Mr. Babic held a meeting with the opposite side in Krajina on the 10th of February, which decided to hold a referendum on the issue on the 22nd and 23rd of February. When this report was written, he and some his followers still expressed their opposition to the plan. However, I have come to the conclusion that I must not allow these criticisms in themselves to block the recommendation itself which this report contains. They nonetheless represent a potential danger for the implementation of the plan and therefore it is even more important for the fears and interests of the Serb community in Krajina to be viewed in their entirety at the Conference on Yugoslavia chaired by Lord Carrington." And I think that this was -- is indeed Lord Carrington's intention. Therefore, does this deny -- is this a disclaimer of your story, the story you tell, that you in fact accepted the plan when it says in this UN Secretary-General report, with all the efforts that were invested and final agreement reached on the part of the Assembly with our maximum efforts in that regard to have the plan implemented although it was quite clear that you and several -- a couple of other followers of yours were opposed to that plan and resisted the plan.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter, as you have stated, is dated the 11th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said the 15th of February.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. So around the 12th or 13th of March, 1992, the municipal assembly of Knin, which I chaired, made a decision by which it accepted the deployment of UN peacekeepers on its territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But that is afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the UN Security Council made the decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
