utterances.text: Yes, after the UN Security Council decided to deploy its peacekeepers, then you at the Knin municipal meeting accepted this, but it was rather a belated decision and represented no relevant factor in the form of being a contribution to the plan's implementation. I assume that that was so.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I receive in -- that is your interpretation. I should like the Trial Chamber to take note of that. After the UN Security Council had accepted the plan, I accepted it too. My resistance was before it had actually gone through in the UN Security Council.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I think we can go back into open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have the documents, Resolution and report?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At the moment, we're searching for the English version in our systems, and I cannot say so, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like the documents be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think they should be exhibited, the Resolution and the UN Secretary-General report that I've just quoted from. And it would be a good thing if you had the Serbian version for you to be able to compare and see that I quoted very precisely. Each word is in its proper place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regardless of the fact that the original is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with them now. There should be a Resolution and a report. If the registrar has them, they could be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the exhibits be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. Resolution 802 dated the 25th of January, 1993, will be Defence Exhibit 66. And the Further Report of the Secretary-General dated the 15th of February, 1992, will be Defence Exhibit 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To go back to the meeting in Igalo and the agreement reached there with Lord Carrington about a ceasefire, you had occasion to hear the tape as well of the conversation between General Kadijevic and the Croatian president, Franjo Tudjman, in which Kadijevic insists upon the fact that the agreement reached with Carrington should be respected. You know the subsequent events that took place. Is it true that the Croatian side yet again did not respect the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you remind me of the date, please? I didn't take part in the agreement, so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Igalo, it took place in November 1991. That was when the meeting was held at which the agreement on a ceasefire was signed and when Kadijevic -- or, as far as I have noted down here, you can -- the date should be checked out. It was the 17th of September, not November. The 17th of September, 1991, was the date. Is it true that the Croatian side once again did not respect the agreement? You listened to the tape, and you know about the events. So is it correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the middle of September, according to my information, the Yugoslav People's Army took -- launched an active operation towards Nis. At the beginning of October, it went towards Zadar and Sibenik. Now, what happened on other battlefronts I can't say with any certainty, but after the middle of the September, the intensity of the armed conflict escalated considerably. Now, who violated the agreement, if that was the date that it was reached, I don't know. What I do know was that there were incidents which broke out in the area of Petrovo Polje and -- Petrovo Polje near Drnis and Molvice in Lika. At Petrovo Polje, what happened was that police groups from Knin started shooting. There was crossfire with the Croatian forces - whether police forces or the guards corps, I don't quite know - but the report said that there was some shooting going on that something was happening down there, I don't know exactly what. And then Frenki's armoured platoon went to Tepljuh and the situation escalated. After that, the Knin Corps reacted with its artillery and fired at the Croatian positions and settlements in Petrovo Polje. That was in September 1991, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you very specifically about the cease-fire agreement and not about the events that took place before the cease-fire agreement was reached, and what I asked you specifically was: Is it true that the Croatian side yet again did not respect the agreement, and you heard the telephone conversation between Kadijevic and Tudjman in which Kadijevic is advocating respect for Carrington's agreement and insisting upon the fact that they ceased their attacks on the barracks to enable the barracks to have water and electricity supplies and to abide by the agreement. So I'm asking you: Is it true that, after the agreement was reached, the Croatian side did not respect it once again?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge and information, I did hear that there were ten or 15 agreements, cease-fire agreements, in the course of that autumn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the 15 agreements of any kind, I'm asking you about the Carrington agreement that the whole world knew about and that Tudjman signed. It wasn't an agreement between two commanders or anything like that, it was signed by Tudjman himself. That's the agreement that I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: M. Babic, if you don't know the answer to a question, just say you don't know and we'll get on more quickly. But if you do know, just try and answer it directly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I try to say what I know about the events of the time. And as for this question, all I can say is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that Kadijevic, in his letter to Lord Carrington on the following day - and this was published in the papers - said that in spite of all assurances by Croatian organs that they had ordered a ceasefire, attacks were still continuing with exceptional force and a remorselessness and that, unfortunately, at 12.00 of the 12th when a complete cease-fire was to have taken effect, the Croatian forces not only did not stop but they intensified their attacks on the JNA. It goes on to say that in Zagreb, Sibenik, Varazdin Petrinja, Vukovar Vinkovci, in the area of Sinj, Skradin, Ogulin and other places, attacks had taken place and not a single JNA facility had been unblocked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think I have already said what I know about these events at the time. I said that in September, there was an intensive blockade and also attacks by Croatian forces on barracks in the towns of Croatia. I knew about this from the media, and this was common knowledge. People talked about. And I have already said this. And I tried to add to this what I myself saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember the decisions on the blocking of all JNA barracks in Croatia? This decision was issued in mid-August 1991, while the decision on attacks on the barracks and all JNA units was made on the 14th of September, 1991, and Carrington responded immediately in order to prevent this, and a few days later the cease-fire agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and I knew about this, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. The events of the 6th of May in Split and Sibenik, which are well known, up until the 25th of July, do you know that in this period there were 126 incidents recorded in Croatia of force used against persons and facilities of the JNA and 22 armed attacks on JNA units were registered, 11 instances of opening fire and physically imperilling barracks, 36 incidents of overstepping of authority?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of such events but I can't tell you any precise data. This was the second stage of the escalation of conflicts after the events of May 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Is it clear from these facts - and these are facts, not somebody's standpoints - that the then-leadership of Croatia, several days before the meeting with Carrington, issued a decision on an all-out attack and the JNA and that what was agreed in Igalo was not respected a single moment, that is, that the leadership of Croatia never had any intention of complying with it. When all these facts are added up and compared, isn't this clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop these speeches. If you want to comment on what the accused has said, you can do so, M. Babic, or we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. What was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When what you yourself say in your reply that you know about, in connection with the decision on blockading barracks, in connection with the decision on attacks throughout Croatia on barracks, after which there followed an intervention by Lord Carrington and Tudjman signed the agreement on a cease-fire which involved the mobilising reservists of the Croatian National Guard and so on and so forth, that the attacks intensified, which is evident from Kadijevic's letter to Lord Carrington written on the following day, and that not for a single moment did they comply with or have any intention of complying with the agreement they had signed with Lord Carrington.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the agreement was reached in September, on the basis of your question, I can say that from the 26th of August, as far as I know, a large-scale intervention by the JNA began in the direction of the territories controlled by the Croatian government and police. I don't know what you want me to do now, whether you want me to make what I know fit into some conclusion of yours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt that's what the accused wants to do, and his conclusions are matters which he can submit to us. They're not matters for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that in 1990 Tudjman, at a meeting with Manovic, Bojkovac and other associates of his, worked out in detail the first stage of the then-concealed covert war against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, I won't put any questions about this, about elements of something you know nothing about. Do you know that when issuing the decision on a forcible secession, the members of the Croatian leadership had a strategy of -- of a simultaneous attack on the JNA in order to stretch out the forces in all places where the JNA was deployed in Croatia to cover as wide a territory as possible and to engage them in a large number of small tasks while prolonging the institutional crisis in the country and obstructing the functioning of the political, economic, and military system in an attempt to limit the JNA in its ability to -- and to attack it? Do you know what was happening at the time? Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know about the preparations of the government of Croatia against the JNA, while I think this is the first thing I heard, it was information that came from the federal secretariat for defence, the information service, and this was the first time that these activities of the Croatian government were presented in detail. That was on the 25th of January, 1991. And I have already spoken of what was being said at the time, what people talked about, that the Croatian government was arming the police and the members of the HDZ, and the ruling party and the then-government of Croatia had a model for ordering relations in Yugoslavia. They openly advocated their own political model, and that was quite clear. I don't know what else you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it correct that after Plitvice, which we have just mentioned, that fresh conflicts broke out, one after another, against Serbian villages? For example, in Glina, Brsadin, there were armed clashes between the Croatian police and the Serbian police and attacks on citizens of Serb nationality where there were dead, wounded, imprisoned? Do you remember anything of this? For example, on the 26th of June, 1991, in Glina and Brsadin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the clash in Glina very well, because after the outbreak of these clashes, I was in the vicinity or, rather, I claim to Glina and I was able to see what was going on there. The special police of the Krajina, Captain Dragan, and armed citizens from Glina were engaged in an armed conflict with the Croatian police and attempting to take over the police station in Glina which until then had been held by the Croatian police. I am well aware of this, but I don't know anything much about the events in Brsadin. What else did you ask me about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you know nothing about this, and you explained that in Glina it was the Serbs who attacked the Croats. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Serbs did not attack the Croats, but the special police of the Krajina and Captain Dragan in particular, were attacking the police station held by the Croatian police in Glina, and they took it over after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was an attempt made to take the village of Mirkovci near Vinkovci on the 22nd of July 1991, where there were also dead and wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were battles in the vicinity of Mirkovci and that the inhabitants, and especially the TO of the village of Mirkovci, were involved and this was well known in public. This was made public Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that they fought there in persistent defend -- effort to defend Mirkovci. And a young girl, I remember, was very popular among the Serbs, she fought on the Serbian side. I don't recall her name now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, since you have just spoken of how the police of the Krajina actually attacked the Croats in Glina --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that it attacked the Croats. I said it attacked the police station in Glina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, the police station. Glina is in Banija, isn't that correct, and there are other places there. Also, is it correct, tell me precisely, that it was you yourself who appointed people, your own people, to leading positions in the area, at the same time dismissing those who were loyal to Jovan Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring first of all to Dvor na Uni, Kostajnica, Petrinja, and Glina, the area of Banija.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session. 18 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the Petrinja municipality, you appointed your colleague president, someone of the same profession as you, Radovan Maljkovic, and that the president of the executive council was Nikola Bandur appointed by you, who is also the president of the Crisis Staff. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Well, I can say it is not correct because a community of local communes of the municipality of Petrinja was set up there and they elected their own president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not appoint your colleague Radovan Maljkovic of the same profession as you as president?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I accepted him as president but he was elected by the people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the barracks in Petrinja, Samarica, and Vasil Gacesa, which is the Petrinja garrison of Colonel Tarbuk, were constantly under the blockade of Croatian forces until the 21st of September, 1991, and that the members of the JNA, even had they wanted to, were unable to be active in the area of Banija but this was the TO commanded by you and your commanders. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say? You said several things here. Can you repeat them one by one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first thing I asked you was did you appoint your colleague, a dentist, as the president of the municipality in Petrinja? You say he was elected by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a psychiatrist, not a dentist, and he was elected by the Assemblymen, that is, by the representatives of the local communes of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I asked you, was it correct that the Petrinja garrison was under the constant blockade of Croatian forces until the 21st of September and that, even had they wanted to, they would not have been able to operate in the area because they were under a blockade and no one was able to leave the barracks, and any activity was done exclusively by the Territorial Defence which was under your command. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town of Petrinja was under the control of the Croatian government. The Petrinja garrison was on the outskirts of the town. What sort of blockade it was under, I cannot know exactly. I know that units of the Petrinja garrison took part in the fighting around Kostajnica and especially in the fighting around Jabukovac. People told me that Captain Letic from that unit commanded the artillery or a tank or something or other and that he had the merit for liquidating the Croatian outpost in Jabukovac which belongs to the municipality of Petrinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's move on. Let's move on. I ask you whether it's correct or not, and you answer not very clearly, so I can't really tell what your answer is.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Put your answers -- put your questions and I will answer each one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the JNA did not take part at all in the fighting around Dvor na Uni, Kostajnica, Glina and Petrinja because the JNA, according to the decision of the Presidency of the SFRY, was exclusively used to create a buffer zone? Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Petrinja garrison took part in the fighting around Dvor, Petrinja -- sorry, around Kostajnica and two other places, but I'm not sure, I don't know about Dvor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you know this, can you tell us when it happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in September, the month of September. Yes, yes, in September 1991. In September 1991. I know about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When in September? When in September?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, starting in September and onwards. Whether it was -- whether it had happened before, I don't know, but people told me this in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how could it happen when the barracks in Petrinja were under a blockade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I know there was a conflict there and that they took part in the fighting. As I said, the barracks of the Petrinja garrison were on the outskirts of Petrinja and some were in other places. You mentioned two other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were two barracks. Petrinja is not New York. And do you know that Colonel Tarbuk, the commander of the Petrinja garrison, from leaders of the civilian authorities that you as the TO commander had appointed, explicitly demanded that the burning and looting of Croatian homes organised by you be stopped?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't organise it, and I am not aware of that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that precisely because of the blockade of the Petrinja garrison in Banija a motorised brigade under the command of Colonel Boric came from another area to take over this function of a buffer zone since the Petrinja garrison was unable to do that as it was under blockade by paramilitary forces of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd heard of Colonel Boric, but where exactly he was engaged, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And is it true, Mr. C-061, that your man, the president of the municipality of Petrinja that we mentioned a moment ago, Dr. Radovan Maljkovic, broke off contacts with the JNA garrison of Colonel Tarbuk, and he wrote a letter to Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, the commander of the Serbian volunteer guards, asking him to come to the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that letter on the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. That is the first time I heard of that letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then tell me, can you explain why you broke off relations with the army and wrote a letter to Arkan? Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't break off our relations with the army at all. We supported the mobilisation, and we felt the JNA was the most powerful force to protect the Serbian people in Krajina, and it was really no reason. It wouldn't be logical, and it's simply not true. We supported the Yugoslav People's Army as the armed force of Yugoslavia, which was under your command, to protect the Serbian people in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've already talked about commanding, so you don't have to mention it each and every time. You learnt your lesson well enough. Tell me, please, is it true that this same Dr. Radovan Maljkovic, at the elections in Krajina at the end of 1993, on behalf of your party, in fact, therefore a close associate of yours, became a deputy in the Assembly of the Republic of Srpska Krajina where he was one of the most extreme -- greatest extremists? The people around you were the most extreme, as can be seen from all the documents. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that Dr. Radovan Maljkovic was elected deputy of the Assembly of the Republic of Srpska Krajina in the constituency of Petrinja and that his nomination had come from the Serbian Democratic Party of Krajina, and the rest are your allegations, which are not true. I can also say the following, and that is why you're mentioning Radovan Maljkovic; he was a political opponent of Borislav Mikelic who was very influential in Petrinja and Banija. So that is my opinion why you are mentioning his name right now, Radovan Maljkovic. Borislav Mikelic was a man who, even before he left the area, had a lot of influence in Petrinja, Kostajnica and Dvor na Uni. He couldn't in Glina because he had a personal opponent there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as Borislav Mikelic is concerned, even in the former Yugoslavia he was one of the most prestigious businessmen and the manager of the largest factory of that time in the country, called Gavrilovic [phoen], so certainly the most influential person in Petrinja as the Petrinja combine by far extended the boundaries of his municipality. Therefore, whether he was influential or not is not a question. He certainly was influential. What was strange about that? The question is how he used that influence, and he used it for a peaceful solution and not for conflict.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he assisted in arming Banija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He told you that. Well, that's fine. Oh, I see that he has merits for that. We'll come to some other questions with respect to Mikelic who engaged in negotiations for a peaceful settlement which you obstructed, as we established yesterday. Is it not clear that everything that you're attributing to the Yugoslav People's Army and the police force of Krajina was actually done or perpetrated by people appointed by you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said what I know about what was done, where it was done, and how it was done, and who was responsible in the chain of command in the areas in which those occurrences happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in answer to the previous question too when I said that you had appointed Maljkovic who was an extremist in your party, you more or less confirmed it because you confirmed that it was upon the proposal of your party that he was elected, as if he was not a member of your leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer to this question about the appointment of this man.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it true that with the assistance of Mile Paspalj, you appointed another colleague of yours by profession, Dusan Jovic, in Glina? Dr. Dusan Jovic who was also president of the Crisis Staff and commander of the Territorial Defence of Glina and president of the War Presidency of Glina? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Dusan Jovic was a gynaecologist, and he was elected president of the municipality by the deputies of the Assembly of the Municipal Assembly of Glina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned him as being in confrontation with Mikelic, and he was also a member of the leadership of your party, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a personal conflict with Mikelic because he married Mikelic's former wife, ex-wife, and he was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party, yes. He was a member of the same party as I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you in that party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what time period?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time when you appointed Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovic was elected president of the municipality by the deputies of the Municipal Assembly. Jovic was appointed commander of the regional TO staff in Banija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who appointed him to that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of July 1991, by the Prime Minister acting as the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it you that appointed him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this a private session or an open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a private session. So you appointed him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I appointed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you appointed him and Maljkovic and the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not Maljkovic. Nor did I appoint Jovic as president of the Assembly but only to this position that I've just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You're using the term "appointing," he was appointed as if he were an observer and you appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's one procedure of the election of the president of the Assembly and another matter is the appointment of the president of the Crisis Staff, which Jovic should have been but he didn't manage to establish command over Dvor na Uni, Kostajnica because of his conflict with Mikelic and with Vajagic, who was commander of the 7th Banija Division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look, I'm talking about Glina now and about Jovic whom you appointed. Didn't you just now mention the municipality of Glina and the crimes and burning of Croatian property in the area, the village of Josevica and Vidusevica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vidusevac? I don't know about the first one, but the other one I saw personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is responsible for this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who was in command of that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in command of that area if it was not the person you had appointed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said exactly how the chain of command worked in that area and at what time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. Is it true that the proclamation of the War Presidency of Glina municipality was signed by that very Dusan Jovic whom you had appointed and who was doing that in accordance with your own policies? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Jovic was president of the Municipal Assembly of Glina and, as such, he could have been the president of the so-called War Presidency, if that was what it was called. So the War Presidency was part of the Municipal Assembly which was acting as the Assembly in conditions of imminent threat of war or state of war. So if he was the president of the Assembly, then he also was the president of the so-called War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So he was the one who wrote this proclamation in the bulletin of the War Presidency of the TO staff of Glina. So TO staff and not the municipality. And you had nominated him. And he says, "How long will you continue to watch the suffering imposed upon us by his -- Tudjman and his Ustashas with indifference, turning a blind eye to it all?" And it is an extremely, extremely inflammatory, I would say, vocabulary. Was that your policy? Was that in harmony with your policy, or did someone from Belgrade, perhaps, have influence over him, or some parallel structure or some Holy Ghost who cropped up in the middle of the night to tell him to do what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about. The aim was to protect the Serbian people in Krajina and not to inflict harm on the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I think that will be enough. But since there is no doubt that you knew about all this, especially as Jovic was a member of the top leadership of your party, how, then, can you speak about chaos in Banija and Kordun when it was you yourself who had control over these areas through these people who you personally had appointed and who behaved in an extreme manner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have that area under control, I was just speaking about facts. I don't know what you mean. How could I have had control over the area when there were command structures, as far as the military command is concerned? As for political -- as for the political, I've already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, fine. Is it true that Dr. Dusan Jovic, that same man, was later appointed Health Minister in your government of SAO Krajina and later the Republic of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaso Lezajic, Dr. Vaso Lezajic was Minister of Health in the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Jovic? Was he -- did he have a position in the government of SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the government of SAO Krajina? I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You don't remember whether Jovic had a position in your government. The Health Minister was Vaso Lezajic. And what was Jovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember that he was in the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you claiming that he was not in the government of SAO Krajina and the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe in the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. He was. And who was Prime Minister at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Jovic was there. When Jovic was in it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. It's possible, but I don't remember. But he certainly was not a member of the government of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. He was possibly a member of the government of the Republic of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Vaso Lezajic was the Health Minister in the government of SAO Krajina and the Republic of Krajina until another set of people took over, so he couldn't have been in that government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he wasn't a minister in that government. You don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a minister in the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yet you were the Prime Minister at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't the Prime Minister of the republic, I was president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. And what kind of links could have the structures in Serbia have had to what was happening in Glina and Banija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I was the one who appointed this Jovic and wrote these proclamations for him and controlled him and did what he did; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were at the top of the command structure, as I have already described it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Your description is your affair. But let's move on. Is it true that upon your initiative at Dvor na Uni, at your personal initiative in Dvor na Uni, as well as in Petrinja and Glina, the president of the municipality, Simo Rajisic, was replaced and in his position your close associate appointed, also from the SDS, Pero Cvjetanovic? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Dvor na Uni, there were two current, two in the SDS and one outside the SDS, Simo Rajisic belonged to the former left wing. The bulk of the SDS in Dvor na Uni was held by a faction in which there was Zunic and others. Pero Cvjetanovic was one faction. He was a founding member of the SDS. He was president of the municipality for a very brief time. And I did not appoint him to that position but the deputies of the Municipal Assembly. As for Petrinja, I said that I didn't appoint anyone over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else did you mention? I asked you what you just confirmed, that you replaced the president of the municipality Simo Rajisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No he didn't. Don't misrepresent the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. We've lost the translation. Would you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you at least confirmed that Pero Cvjetanovic, whom you appointed to replace Simo Rajisic, belonged to your party, a member of the leadership of your party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A member of the party whose president was Dr. Jovan Raskovic, and he was one of the close associates and founding members of Raskovic [as interpreted]. I did not replace him, nor did I appoint the other person to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there's no dispute that he was a member of the top leadership of your party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the party the president of which was Mr. -- Dr. Jovan Raskovic. And he was a member of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Tell me, please, you mentioned Goran Hadzic somewhere. You said, in a denigrating term, that he was a warehouse guard, a warehouse clerk.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was embarrassed to speak of his qualifications, but when I was asked to do so, I had to say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you felt that his qualifications were such that he was not capability of performing a certain public office? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he was an eloquent politician, and I didn't link his qualifications to his political activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So if you had such an attitude towards his qualifications, how then, when you replaced Matijasevic from the position of the president of the Assembly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That is not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you appoint Mile Paspalj president of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the Assembly elected him to that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. The Assembly elected.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every president is elected by the Assembly. That is, the deputies of the Assembly. What preceded this was the following: As the previous president of the Assembly was Velibor Matijasevic, who used to be president of the municipality of Glina, there was an internal clash between Matijasevic and a group around Mile Paspalj and Borisav Jovic, and this conflict was resolved in such a way that Matijasevic was replaced and Jovic was elected to the position of president of the Assembly. In view of the fact that I held Matijasevic in high esteem as a lawyer, an activist in Banija, I knew him from the time of the founding of the Serbian Democratic Party, I favoured his election as president of the Assembly of SAO Krajina, and I was supported by some other deputies, and he was elected president of the Assembly of SAO Krajina. And then what happened was that he fell under the influence of Martic, Dusan Starevic, and some other people who were under the control of Jovica Stanisic, and then he obstructed Assembly meetings being scheduled. I said that already in the autumn of 1991, when I was supposed to go to the first meeting with Wijnaendts in Paris, he scheduled a meeting of the Assembly at which the Prime Minister, that is me, was supposed to submit a report, and I said how this was resolved through your intervention and that of Jovica Stanisic. Later on, when the government asked for an Assembly session, he refused to convene an Assembly session, and that is why I went to Banija to seek political support to convene the Assembly and to renew the institutions of SAO Krajina, and on the 21st of November, 1991, the government asked for an Assembly session to be convened. The deputies came -- the majority of deputies came to attend, but Matijasevic, the vice-president of the Assembly, Drago Zecevic, the vice-president of the Assembly from Lapac, obstructed this. And then the majority of deputies decided that the Assembly should sit nevertheless, and they elected a new president and that was Mile Paspalj. So Paspalj was president of the Regional Board of the Serbian Democratic Party in Glina. Because he had very strong political influence in Banija and as Matijasevic was from Banija too, the political formula was that people in position should not all be from one part of SAO Krajina but that they should be evenly -- that all parts of SAO Krajina should be evenly represented in the political bodies of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time has come to adjourn, if we look at the clock. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. May, that we're still in private session. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly from the explanation you gave, Matijasevic was a prominent member of the SDS and, as such, elected to the post of president of the Assembly, as you yourself explained. And then you went on to say that he linked up with Martic and began working in a way that you didn't find suitable, and that was why he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained why he was replaced, why Matijasevic was replaced; because he did not attend the Assembly meeting, and he obstructed the Assembly session. Now, how he became linked to the parallel structures or the way in which Jovica Stanisic wielded influence on him, I've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I didn't hear you explain that. I don't know how he came to influence him or why the President of the Assembly was a parallel structure for you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that at the beginning or, rather, sometime around the 12th of October, 1991, around that date anyway, a meeting was held at your office, or perhaps it was a day before that, but that's the general time frame, and that it was a preparatory meeting for the SAO delegation and Serbian region of Slavonia and Baranja to attend negotiations within the frameworks of The Hague conference prior to our departure for Paris together with Ambassador Wijnaendts. And during that meeting, I put forward to you the fact that the president of the Assembly, Matijasevic, had sent out an invitation for me to attend the meeting and that I was to table a report as Prime Minister. And I said that I could not be in two places at the same time, I couldn't be in Knin and in Paris at one and the same time, and you said that you knew nothing about that. To that, I answered that Jovica Stanisic knew. You left the room, and a little while later, the Assembly was cancelled and I went to Paris for the negotiations without having any burdens or any obligation to table a report to the Assembly. So that was my knowledge of how Jovica Stanisic influenced Matijasevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what Jovica Stanisic has got to do with Matijasevic is we insisted upon you attending the peace negotiations in Paris and that was the priority rather than the attendance of your Assembly meeting which you could hold any time you liked, and the Paris conference couldn't be held any time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think Matijasevic explained that that was more important, or whatever he did, actually, I don't know, but that was the outcome at my intervention with you and the fact that Jovica Stanisic said that he could do that, he could wield influence on Matijasevic, and he did indeed do so, it appears.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I influenced Matijasevic to defer the Assembly meeting for you to be able to go to attend the peace negotiations in Paris with Ambassador Wijnaendts; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me then, please, as you had replaced Matijasevic, what were the circumstances under which Matijasevic was subsequently killed a short while later?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Matijasevic I don't think died soon after the 20th of November. Actually, I don't know when he was killed. But a little while later, I heard -- I don't know exactly, but I heard people from Banija say that he had gone to have an inspection of the communal infrastructure or water supply system. Now, whether he was at that time the director, I'm not quite sure, but that he was killed somewhere out there. That's what I heard. And later on, I met his parents on one occasion and they talked about it but didn't go into the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can I conclude from what you're saying, then, when you link it all up and recapitulate, that all the people that disagreed with you, that did not agree with you, according to your criteria, were ranked among the formations of some parallel structure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A parallel structure is a concept of the military line and political line, military or political chain, that you wielded influence over and were in command of on the territory of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you have just construed that parallel structure concept. But as we're still in private session, I'm going to ask you a few questions with respect to your interview, the interview that was otherwise played here. It is on page 02034458, as provided by the opposite side over there. And in that interview of yours, you state the following -- I'm just going to read several extracts. I see it's rather a long one. It is three pages of a newspaper long. The weekly magazine Nin published it. And you say: "The Serbian Democratic Party politically succeeded in uniting the people --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be of assistance. It is tab 26, Exhibit 352.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The Serb Democratic Party politically succeeded in uniting the Serb people within the Avnoj boundaries of Croatia, the anti-fascist council boundaries, and the SDS succeeded because quite simply it was stated that the need arose for the articulation of Serb consciousness in the area." Are those your words?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date was the interview?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interview appeared in the weekly Nin, and as far as I was able to gather, it was the 18th of January, 1991. That was the date.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you go on to say: "It is the task of the SDS to further establish overall democratic relations within the Serb nation." Are those your words?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are my words, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy of the interview. It will be much easier for him. If you would take him to the place that you're referring to, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I read that from page 2. The second page, paragraph one, column one, and this is column two where you give your explanations that are contrary to the ones you are stating here and now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's get the passage again that you were asked to comment on. Have you got it, M. Babic? "Serbian Democratic Party politically succeeded in uniting the people of the anti-fascist boundaries and succeeded because, quite simply, it was stated that the need arose for the articulation of Serb consciousness in the area." Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I said articulate. I think there was a question of some sort of articulation of views, and I'm talking about the political consciousness, political awareness and that kind of articulation. In the political sense of the word. Could you help me, please? I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The task of the SDS is to establish overall democratic relations within the Serbian nation...." That was your ambition, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS was set up for the area of the entire SFRY. So throughout the territory where the Serb people lived. And it was defined in its programme as such, that it would support the interests of the Serb people and implement the democratic relations in society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, now, how far is what you're saying now different from what you wrote then, or the other way round? You say here, and that is in the middle column of the article, newspaper article on page 2, which says: "The HDZ as the political will of the Croatian people, which quasi-democratic relations were established in Croatia, in which more democracy is meant for one people; i.e., more rights to the Croats than to the Serbs. And that was particularly manifest in the Croatian Sabor Assembly whereby the HDZ was supported by all the Croat nationalist parties in this endeavour and also the so-called left bloc which was turned into an Assembly and that would make the political interests of all citizens more difficult but it fixates the interests of one people, the Croatian people." And then it says: "Through such political action --" and then it says in brackets, "(through the Croatian Assembly) national torture of one peoples over another was effected so that the Serb people had to find new political instruments in order to protect its equality. This instrument was found in the institution of the Serb National Council, formerly the Serb Assembly."

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already talked about that. We defined the Serb Assembly in Srb as a second part of the Croatian Sabor or Assembly. So we defined the HDZ policy and the majority in the Croatian parliament and defined it as Croato-centralism and nationalism. That was the definition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was your definition that a national torture of one people over another was being effected.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the term I used, torture, because we considered that Croato-centrism and hegemony was being effected through the centralist system, that is to say, through the Croatian parliament or Sabor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, does that then mean that these positions of yours were not - how shall I put it - dictated from Belgrade at all? You are now explaining to us that that's how you saw the situation, how you felt, what your sentiments were, and that you reacted in that fashion. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards our political relationship towards the HDZ and towards the majority in the parliament, I explained that. I said we waged a fervent political struggle with the HDZ and the parties that gained the majority in parliament and that you became involved in that political struggle by provoking incidents and bringing that political struggle to a head and that this brought about an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So it wasn't you who caused all the incidents with what we've discussed a moment ago with your commanding, et cetera. It was somebody else that gave rise to those incidents. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that as of 1990, the events that followed and the information that I have I presented here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the right-hand paragraph in the middle, you say: "Therefore the Serbian Autonomous Province in Krajina was not the result of anybody's whim or armed struggle but we could talk about a logical continuity. It was not the result of banditry." And then you go on to say: "We have nothing against Croatians waging their own national drives. We have nothing against their independence either, but on Croatian ethnic ground." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I thought at the time and you convinced me that that was right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say I convinced you. When did I convince you? This is the 18th of January, 1991 that we're talking about. All right, all right, if you say I convinced.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with Borisav Jovic, when I had a meeting, I had a meeting with you later on and you said that that was our legitimate right and you said that you would defend and protect us in furthering those rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I quoted the principles of the Yugoslav state Presidency which the Presidency had determined when it was in full composition with the presence of all the leading figures in Yugoslavia of the day.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that sometimes, and very often, there were differences between your public declarations and what you in fact went about doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ah. So you know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I talked about the facts and my knowledge of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief in connection with this interview, you explained that it was the journalist by the name of Grubac who in fact influenced you and had you present your views in this particular fashion.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about Grubac not only in connection with this newspaper article but I said I had known him from 1990 onwards and that he did wield influence on me, especially in the spring of 1991, because he demanded that I attack Vuk Draskovic and that this was following your instructions, that you wanted me to do so and that I should write letters of support to a counter rally of the SPS during the march demonstrations along those lines, and that is how I spoke of Grubac's influence upon him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, tell me, did I ask you for any support?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that you had asked for me to attack Vuk Draskovic by making statements, that that was something you asked in March and that you had asked me to write a letter to the participants of a rally at the Usce with respect to the 9th of March demonstrations held in 1991, and I was invited to attend the meeting by your associate Dusan Markovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how was I able to ask anything of you through Grubac when I didn't know Grubac at the time and I don't remember meeting him more than once or twice later on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said the following, and I know that. He was close to Snezana Aleksic and she was very close to you. You had family ties and she was close to the leadership of the party led by your wife, and Grubac was also on close terms with Goran, your chef de cabinet. I think they had discussions about me too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now if you say that he was close to my wife's party, you're talking about the Yugoslav Leftist Party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Snezana was one of the leaders of the Yugoslav Left Party and she told me that she was close to you privately, and her office was in the Central Committee building. When he asked me to write my speech for the rally held at Usce, and I dictated the speech to him over the phone, he gave the speech to Snezana Aleksic and she sent it on further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, now, please, as we're not disputing the fact that this interview was given on the 18th of January, 1991, that is not in dispute, tell me, do you perhaps know that the Yugoslav Left Party was formed in 1994? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Snezana Aleksic was a member of the party later on, and she had family ties, close family ties to you at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let's just establish this fact first.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And she gave us your home telephone number. That's how Grubac came by your home telephone number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who handed out my private telephone number at home. That's not the subject of our discussion or my cross-examination of you here, whether somebody gave you -- provided you with my telephone number at home or not. What I wanted to note was that the Yugoslav Leftist Party was founded in 1994, and we're talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Aleksic was a member later on of the Yugoslav Left Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me this: Is it true that when you were replaced at the Glina Assembly session, that you were -- that you replaced Ljubica Solaja straight away and you took over the leadership of the SDS in Krajina and Ljubica Solaja later joined the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the first news I had that I had been replaced in Glina was over Belgrade television. That's the first point. Second, Madam Ljubica Solaja had been replaced by the majority of Presidency members. I took part in the meeting. I think it was at the end the April. And there were two particular events that forerunners to this. One was Solaja's and Cubrilo's attempts to set up a Serb army in Kosovo but she wasn't replaced because of that but later on because she supported by Zdravko Zecevic who was our political adversary, and that's why the majority of members of the regional SDS board for Krajina had them replaced. So this was the regional branch of the SDS for Krajina that took this decision. And after she was replaced, I became president of the Regional Board of the SDS for Krajina. And after that, she left and joined the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Ljubica Solaja was replaced and you took her place as president. You assumed the post of president. But that was not through your activities but through the activities of the LDS leadership. You just seemed to be the object of all this, not the subject.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was the subject too. She couldn't have just been dismissed through my own personal will but through the will of the other members of the Assembly. I wasn't able to replace her myself or appoint myself either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, as I wish to ask a few more questions which are linked to -- which were linked to something that was discussed in open session, I think that we could now move back into open session. May we? Because I would like to ask the witness whether one point he made is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that part of the open session -- when we were in open session, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we talked about some issues from the letter of the retired General -- Lieutenant General Djujic. So I want to put just one question in connection with this. Is what I'm going to read now correct, what he says in his letter? We have already explained how he was appointed, what he wrote about this, and then he goes on to say: "I have been performing this duty from the 1st of October, 1991 --" he's referring to the duty of commander of the TO -- "until the 25th of November, 1991. I was dismissed from this post on the 25th of November, 1991, through the decision of the president of the government of the SAO Krajina, Milan Babic." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Ilija Djujic, as far as I know, resigned. His resignation was accepted, and he received the appropriate decision in the appropriate form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You are not answering my question directly, but I understand your answer. Tell me now, please, is it correct what he says here, that the reason for his dismissal was twofold, first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No, the witness didn't say, and you mustn't misrepresent what a witness says. What he said was that the man resigned. You can put, if you want, what was the reason for his resignation. You can put that, but you can't put that it was a dismissal, because the witness doesn't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I am not claiming anything myself, I am simply reading from what he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can you put to the witness what you want to put, but don't misrepresent what he says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. May. I am only quoting from the statement of General Djujic and asking the witness whether it is correct, because the reasons the witness says he was not dismissed but that he resigned -- he himself says he was dismissed, but the witness says he resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the reasons that he enumerates correct? And he lists two reasons: "First because Babic did not agree with me, and the standpoint of the General Staff of the JNA, that the manoeuvring units of the Territorial Defence should be resubordinated to the JNA commands in this area." That's number one. And number two: "Because Babic asked of me that the Territorial Defence on its own initiative attack and take over Skradin, and this is something I did not agree with, among other reasons because Skradin is inhabited by a majority Croatian population." Is this correct, what General Ilija Djujic wrote?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had resigned because of his illness, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I've told you what he says the reasons were.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with this, but we'll go into private session first. 4 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. M. Babic, you deal with this matter of General Djujic resigning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know is the following, not in connection with his resignation but in connection with the problem about resubordinating the Territorial Defence units: After General Ilija Djujic took up his post in early October 1991, he initiated a meeting with General Vukovic and myself, which was held in Benkovac, and he asked that this relationship be resolved, that is, that the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina be the superior command for the Territorial Defence units on the ground also. This was not the case. The superior command for the Territorial Defence on the ground were the JNA commands, and General Vukovic said that this had nothing to do with him, that he was not in charge of this, that this should be resolved in the General Staff. This was one of the topics I discussed with General Adzic. General Adzic said, "No, there will be no changes. Things will stay as they were. The units of the Territorial Defence must remain under JNA command." And that is the only matter I discussed with Djujic in this connection, and this was around the 10th of October, 1991. I never even mentioned to General Djujic at that time while he was there that Skradin should be taken. I know about an operation that was supposed to take place in order to take Skradin, but that was in 1993. I know there was a plan that the Serbian army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina should take Skradin, but it's not true that I spoke of this in 1991 to Djujic. It is true that Djujic said that he was resigning because he was ill, and this is mentioned in the decision that was issued on his -- on the termination of his duty.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume we need no longer remain in closed session, Mr. May, but let us just clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is not correct that the first reason was that you refused to have the Territorial Defence subordinated to the JNA and that you insisted it should be under your command and not under the command of the JNA, which was in accordance with the legislation of Yugoslavia, that it should be commanded by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My idea was that it should first be constituted as an independent military formation which could operate in cooperation with JNA units, but this could not happen for two reasons. First because of the principle of a single chain of command in the SFRY, there could be -- there could not be two parallel chains of command. And secondly, because you did not permit any autonomous government or authority in the Krajina in relation to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he says quite the opposite here. He says you did not allow the Territorial Defence to be subordinated to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible for me to prevent this. I'm telling you what my political idea was to begin with, but I was unable to implement this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that what is said here about the attack on Skradin is also not true, but General Djujic will probably be able to testify to this himself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may continue in open session, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we leave there, I've been referred to page -- I'm sorry, Exhibit 352, tab 22, as the relevant document dealing with the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 72, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 72, dealing with the resignation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say, then, that he was not dismissed but that he resigned. Kruschev also resigned because of old age and illness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment by you. You should look at Exhibit 352, 72 -- tab 72.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in late September 1990, in only two days in Petrinja, over a hundred innocent Serbs were arrested and mistreated. After this, about 400 women and children of Serb ethnicity hid, because they were afraid, in the barracks of the Petrinja garrison.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information on the arrest of the Serbs in Petrinja and their taking refuge in the garrison in early October 1990 was told me by Miss Milena Tanjga during a meeting when the delegation from Croatia and from the federal government was staying in Knin, and Mrs. Tanjga insisted that the representatives of the SAO Krajina -- I apologise, of the municipality of Knin who took part in the negotiations, should not continue the talks until, as she said, "the hostages were released." That's what she called the arrested Serbs in Petrinja. And the president of the Knin municipality said this to the Croatian and the federal delegations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you are now introducing Mrs. Milena Tanjga, can you just explain to us what she was doing and what post she held at the time. Was she also a member of your government or what was she?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, Ms. Milena Tanjga was a journalist, a correspondent of Nova Macedonija from Zagreb. Then she went to Knin. She was the wife of a military officer and -- a colonel, and he was on good terms with -- with Mikelic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now that we are referring to this arrest of hundreds of innocent Serbs in Petrinja and the women and children fleeing and taking refuge in the garrison, are you aware that this action by the Croatian forces gave rise to real panic among the Serbs, who started to flee from their homes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any details, but I do know that not only in the area of Petrinja but also in the area of Dvor na Uni, Glina and the entire area, there were clashes between armed Serbs and the Croatian police. Who armed these Serbs I don't know exactly, but it's true that there were clashes, that there was a lot of confusion, that there were demonstrations, and that people did take refuge in the Petrinja garrison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this fact familiar to you, because it was common knowledge at the time and many people talked about it, that the Serbs in that area had no weapons whatsoever apart from several hunting rifles and licensed pistols?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March in your cabinet, I heard from the outgoing Minister of the Interior, Radmilo Bogdanovic, that before March 1991 he had sent 500 pieces of weapons to Banija. When exactly he sent them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You couldn't have heard this from Radmilo Bogdanovic, but we shall be able to clarify where you got such ideas from. But as we are now talking about the arrests and people fleeing and taking refuge in the barracks and so on and so forth, on the basis of what are you saying that Martic, the Serbian DB, the JNA, or the Belgrade media had anything at all to do with these events? Anyone, apart from the local people, the SDS activists who were appointed to leading positions in the manner that we attempted to clarify in private session?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the events and incidents in 1990, especially in October, I have said everything I know about the events in Northern Dalmatia, Lika, the area of Knin and Banija, and what I know is what I have said here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the events in the area of Banija and Petrinja were reported to the federal government and the federal Ministry of the Interior and the Presidency of the SFRY by Borislav Mikelic, the then president of the Socialist Party of Croatia which was Yugoslav oriented?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what he reported, but I know that Borislav Mikelic held a rally in Banski Grabovac in Banija at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on the occasion of these events in the areas of Petrinja and Banija, a special delegation of the Yugoslav government arrived, headed by the vice-president or, rather, the Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandar Mikelic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This delegation visited all the Serbian municipalities and all the municipalities in which there had been incidents in Northern Dalmatia and Banija, and this happened around the 6th of October 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on, Vasil Tupurkovski, a member of the Presidency of the SFRY, came to the area. He was a representative of Macedonia in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Vasil Tupurkovski visited Banija, but I know that he did come to Knin and he talked to the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he take action to calm down the situation? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did try to calm down the situation, but he was told by the President of the municipality of Knin that the president of the municipality of Knin had no influence on the armed incidents taking place in the area of Knin and that he was unable to control them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you do anything to calm the situation in Banija? Did you appear in the area? Did you go there? Did you hold any one of these speeches that nobody has ever heard about about peace?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't go to Banija. No, I wasn't in Banija at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you wish to assert that some sort of representatives from Belgrade were spreading fear in the area of Banija and Kordun?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know about the events in Banija and Kordun I have already said. What I know about the influence of Belgrade and you and Jovica Stanisic in those days, as well as the media in Belgrade, I've already testified about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned several times what the Belgrade media published. Among other things, they reported on the Assembly session of Krajina that we have mentioned. Also the events that really took place. Do you have any examples of the Belgrade media making up events, the events that they wrote about, especially regarding the suffering of the population over there? Did they make things up? Do you have an example of a fabrication that was published so that we can look into that too?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
