utterances.text: The Belgrade media exaggerated things, especially around Pakrac. I have already mentioned here in this courtroom the name of Savo Bosanac and some other people who were killed in Pakrac at the beginning of March 1991. Later on, it was established that this was not true. The Belgrade media constantly, in their features, referred to events from the Second World War and linked them and the new Croatian authorities to the Ustasha crimes. Allow me to answer. Allow me to answer. Through the parallel structure, you manufactured incidents which provoked reaction and fear among the Serb population and intensified intervention by the Croatian police, and this went, spiralled up into intolerance, violence, and eventually war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. On the 15th of February, 1990, by physical force of policemen, the rally of Serbs in Karlovac was prevented, and the rally was against the Ustasha movement and for Yugoslavia. This was prior to the formation of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from people who were organising that rally in Karlovac that they were not allowed to hold it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what has Belgrade got to do with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with any details regarding those events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 4th of March, 1990, a rally was held, a large rally, at Petrova Gora. Among other speakers were Milka Korfrun [phoen], a well-known anti-fascist and a Croat by ethnicity, a Croatian politician at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. I was a participant at that rally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why such a reaction to the resurrection of the Ustasha movement, the ghosts from the Second World War as early as March 1990? How come there was this rally in Petrova Gora? Was that manufactured by the media in Serbia and the parallel structures?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just said was the description of the media in Serbia of the all-Serb rally in Zagreb in the Lisinski hall [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 17th of March in Topusko, a group of intellectuals independently formed the Sabomirka [phoen] Cultural Society and the first magazine in the Cyrillic script after 30 years?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not after 30 years. I know about it. Before that there was Prosjet that was published, a journal of the Serbian Cultural Society, Prosjet, based in Zagreb. So up to '71. In 1971, this journal stopped being published in Cyrillic. So if that was 30 years, yes. Twenty years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was twenty years. Fine, then, after 20 years. And why did Prosjet stop being published in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the work of the Serbian Cultural Society Prosjet in Zagreb was frozen after the events of 1971, that is, the clashes when the Croatian Matica, a literary association, became a political organisation and the Cultural Society Prosjet also became a political organisation. And then the authorities reacted both towards Matica Hrvatska and towards the Serbian Cultural Society Prosjet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's leave that now. Let's put it aside. Do you know that in 1990, in the territory of Slunj municipality, there were about 400 registered Ustashas living there and that, after a short training course, they were given weapons and uniforms of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any detailed information about Ustashas, and I don't know about that case in Slunj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About those 100 Ustashas from Slunj, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that in mixed environments in which there was no hostility, such as Cetingrad, Rakovica, Liganj [phoen], there was so-called stations of the ZNG set up, and their ranks consisted mostly of good-for-nothings and criminals and idlers and Ustashas and the like?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That members of the National Guards Corps of Croatia as an armed formation of Croatia were in Slunj and Cetingrad in November 1991 is something I do know. I was told about that by people from Kordun. And against those formations and against the Croatian population, Cedo Bulat intervened, captured the town of Slunj, and I know there was fighting around Cetingrad, and the area was taken control of, and there were very few members of the guards there or Croats, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the Serbs in Kordun organise themselves in view of these events simply to save their lives or did they make up these dangers that were threatening them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs organised themselves to protect their areas in the ways I have already described, and I also explained who organised them to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that precisely when these so-called outposts were formed in these mixed environments that I have listed, that then Serbs with hunting weapons, out of fear of a repetition of 1941 when several thousand Serbs were killed by the Ustashas in their homes, organised village guards so that these bandits couldn't enter Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that hunting weapons, and particularly carbines manufactured in the Zastava factory in Kragujevac, were sold through the company Loris in Belgrade. They were on sale in Northern Dalmatia and Lika in 1990 and people purchased those weapons. How they bought hunting weapons in the area around Slunj, I don't know exactly, in 1990. But I do know that in 1992, that is as from August, I have information that to that area weapons were delivered via Jovica Stanisic, the DB, and from Serbia through Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile Grbic from Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that at the time in Kordun there wasn't even a branch of the SDS, but the Serbs mostly voted for the SDP as an Independent Yugoslav Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are events from April and May of 1990. The Serbian Democratic Party was poorly organised in Kordun, and the Yugoslav Independent Democratic Party was organised there, headed by Mile Dakic, and also the League of Communists of Croatia, that is the Party of Democratic Change. They were most successful at the elections held in Croatia in April and May 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When we're talking about the fears of the people in Kordun and the formation of the National Guards Corps in these mixed settlements, those village guards that were organised, were they perhaps also organised under some influence from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatians started forming the guards corps as early as 1991. I don't know exactly when they started, but it was the formation of the army of the republic of Croatia within the competence of the Ministry of Defence. Village guards guard duty was held even before the referendum of Serb autonomy in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did anyone from Belgrade take part perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In organising the village guards before the 11th of August, I don't know whether anyone from Belgrade took part. Belgrade took a very active part as from the 11th or 12th of August, encouraging the Serbs, representatives of the Serbs in Croatia, to persevere with respect to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. their political demands, with the promise that the Yugoslav People's Army would protect their political struggle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, as you keep repeating one and the same sentence, you don't need to repeat it every single time you're giving an answer. Do you -- let us take it that you've already said it. Is it known that upon the initiative of the Muslim Bosniak organisation from Velika Kladusa --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what are you talking about? What are you criticising the witness for for repetition, or is it evidence you don't approve of; is that the problem? In that last response, I don't see any repetition.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, he keeps repeating, with respect to everything he has to say, that it was some sort of a parallel structure that he made up, even when that has nothing to do with the question, and he simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt before you go on. You asked him: "Did anyone from Belgrade take part perhaps?" And his answer was: "I don't know whether anyone took part, but it took an active part, Belgrade, from the 11th or 12th of August, encouraging the Serbs, the representatives of Serbs in Croatia, to persevere with respect to their political demands, with the promise that the Yugoslav People's Army would protect their political struggle." That's his answer. And to criticise him because it's a repetition, it seems to me, is wholly wrong. Now, if you would simply restrict your questions to questions, we would all get on better and you would have more time, instead of delivering, as you do, a running commentary on what the witness says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, through a number of questions, we have addressed the position of the Yugoslav People's Army which was separating the opposing parties and which were seeking to calm the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you say, Mr. Milosevic. We will in due course hear your arguments about it and we'll look at the rest of the evidence. Then we'll decide. But for you to issue a running commentary, as you do, upon the witness's evidence, frequently turning it, or trying to turn it in your own favour, isn't going to assist. Now, you've got two hours, 40 minutes left, so let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask you to check the time, please, and to compare the time used by the examination-in-chief. I think it was a little longer than you said. But you have the information, and you can check it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question is: Do you know that upon the initiative of the Muslim Bosniak organisation from Velika Kladusa, Sead Kajtezovic, and the Serbian Democratic Party from Vojnici and Slunj headed by Mile Bosnic, because of the danger of the outbreak of conflicts, negotiations were conducted between the political leaderships of these parties which were later joined by the SDA and the HDZ from the municipalities of Slunj, Velika Kladusa, and Vojnici and Vrginmost. Do you know about that? Are you aware of these efforts of various parties to cooperate amongst themselves, including the SDS, the HDZ, the SDA, and the Bosniak Muslim organisation from Velika Kladusa, and the others that I have mentioned from the municipalities of Slunj, Velika Kladusa, Vojnici and Vrginmost, the aim being to maintain peace in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In later years I heard from someone that there were such talks, but I am not aware of any details. I do know that Mile Bosnic used to work in Velika Kladusa in the combine that was led by Fikret Abdic. That is Agrokomerc, which was managed by Fikret Abdic, and I know that he knew him. He was part of his board of management in his factory and that he knew some people there. He told me later. Now, whether he took part in those negotiations with the Muslim Bosniak organisation and the others that you have listed, I don't know about that. Bosnic did not talk to me about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that those talks and their mutual contacts, the aim of which was not to have any disturbances or conflicts, were interrupted by the activities of the Croatian police when they beat up precisely the participants, that is Momir Lazic, Lazo Dragicevic, Janko Jerkovic, Mile Bosnic, and another two priests of the Serbian Orthodox Church?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the role of Mile Bosnic, Momir Lazic, Dragicevic, and the priests had in connection with talks with people from the parties of Zazine Krajina, but I do know during the events in Plitvice, that is the 31st of March, 1991, these three men set off from Vojnici towards Plitvice via Slunj and that they were arrested there by the Croatian police and detained and that they were physically mistreated and moved to the prison in Karlovac, that they were beaten in Slunj, and then they were moved to the prison in Karlovac where they were more leniently treated and, after that, released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. They beat them with boots and rifle butts, and they congratulated their Easter.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were treated very brutally. I heard from Bosnic and Lazic, and I wondered how he survived, because he's a weak and thin man. Lazic was larger. So I even joked, because I said he was fatter so he managed to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that up to then the Serbs hadn't made a single incident until these people were mistreated and beaten in this way, what you yourself have exceptionally on this occasion confirmed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were events of the 31st of March, 1991. There were many events that preceded this, so I don't know what exactly you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was saying that there were no incidents up to then. I'm talking about the municipalities of Slunj, Vojnici, Velika Kladusa and Vrginmost, where all the parties, Muslim, Croatian and Serbian, sought all together to maintain stability, peace, and tolerance and avoid anything from happening.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a rather complicated question, so I don't really know what your concrete question is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the Serbs, until then, had not caused any incidents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the incidents in 1990, those at the beginning of 1991. I don't know which particular incidents you're referring to. I'm not talking only about Glina and Plitvice but about Slunj, Velika Kladusa, Vojnici.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Vojnici is concerned, Vrginmost, I don't recollect any particular incidents, namely the president of the municipality of Vojnic, Mile Vuckovic, pursued a tactical policy, if I can call it that. He recognised and was even a member of the Assembly of SAO Krajina, and at the same time, the police in Vojnici was receiving salaries from the MUP of Croatia. So he managed to balance things out until the events in Plitvice. And then he protested resolutely and wrote a letter of protest regarding the Bosnic and Lazic and Dragicevic case and the case involving those priests as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that very soon after that, one of the negotiators on the part of the HDZ became casualty, a Croat and member of the government of the ruling party, who was beaten up at the Assembly meeting in Slunj, and he had to leave Slunj after that. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that that was when a witch-hunt was started of the Serbs that were starting to flee and that the first casualties fell? And I'll mention Janko Jerkovic from Vaganjci who was stabbed, Cedo Biga from Grabovac. Then there was Kotur. And then Basnija Niksic [phoen] from Slunj, two other young men, Slobodan Devic and Popovic, were killed on the spot and thrown on a rubbish heap. Nino Vidojevic was another one. They extinguished cigarettes on his body. Do you know that there was this general witch hunt? First of all caused by the beatings and then by the reprisals on both Serbs and Croats who had taken part in the negotiations in the interests of finding a peaceful settlement, and that all this was done by the Croatian police? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't know about these negotiation or who took part in them or how they evolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What about the civilians who had taken up arms to defend their own homes and establish this Serb army of Krajina? Did they come from Belgrade as the occupiers and creators of a Greater Serbia or were they from the villages of Krajina, regardless of which villages?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you talking about now? Are you talking about the negotiations with the Muslims, the events in 1990 and 1991? What are you thinking of quite specifically?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Croatia-061, I'm talking about a general reign of terror that was rampant in the area, and as we've passed through a series of examples, I'm asking you whether the civilians who had taken up arms to defend their own homes and later on organise the Serbian army of Krajina, did they come from Belgrade as occupiers? Is that what you're saying? Or were they from the Krajina villages and took up arms to defend themselves, your formations, the ones that you're mentioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are a series of assertions there. The first assertion is that there was a reign of terror. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the month of October, the incidents that took place were interpreted as being terror on the part of the Croatian authorities by the media. Now, what happened in actual fact in October 1990, I have already explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the Serb army. Well, the Serb army of Krajina was established, institutionally speaking, in May 1992. It's very difficult to answer that question, Your Honours, because the events of 1990 and 1991 and the creation of the Serb army in 1992, all this -- well, actually, I really would like to answer the question but it's a very complex question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Wait a moment. The next point that was made was that the civilians took up arms to defend their own homes and later to organise the Serbian army of Krajina. Do you agree that that is what's happened or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990, what happened was that the civilians bought hunting weapons, and I've already talked about that. In 1991, the weapons were handed out and so-called volunteer units were organised by the DB of Serbia, the Serbian state security, and I talked about that too. The Serbian army of the RSK institutionally speaking was constituted by the Assembly of the RSK itself on the 18th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the third point that was made was this, or the third question: Did they -- these come from Belgrade? Did people come from Belgrade as occupiers or was it a local effort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have spoken about this. As of August, I said which people came in, how they came, what their assignment was, and what they did when they got there. So specifically speaking, from April 1991, they came in to organise a Serbian paramilitary, a paramilitary army in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that they started coming in April, some people over there came in to help you. And what were you doing until April? What happened until April 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've been speaking about that in great detail for days now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As you've been speaking about that specifically and in detail, let's move on. Just give me a very precise, concrete answer. This is a concrete question, we don't need a speech to answer it. Did one single Minister of Defence, the Minister of the Police, the commander of the Main Staff, were any one of these who were people born outside Krajina, throughout the whole time, 1990, 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, any of these people, any of these leading officials, were they born outside Krajina, a single one of them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Minister of the Interior, the Ministers of the Interior -- well, I have to think about this. It's a long period of time you're asking me about and many people, so I have to recall each one separately. You asked me about a whole series of people, a large number of people, so I have to do my best to recollect each one of them. The ministers. Let's see, the Ministers of the Interior. Who were they in the SAO Krajina and the RSK? Yes, they were born in the Krajina area. What else did you say? The Defence Ministers you mentioned. Let's see about them. The Defence Minister Tarbuk, Milan Tarbuk, he was the minister from November 1991. I assume, I'm not quite sure but I assume he was born in Kordun or he originated from Kordun. And the other Defence Minister - what was his name? - of the RSK, in Hadzic's RSK? He was an admiral. I don't know where he was from exactly. What was his name? It's just slipped my mind. The Defence Minister later on was Rade Tanjga, and I think he was born in Ocestovo village, close to Knin. Then there was Minister Milan Suput. I think he was born in the Lika region. So that's as far as the Ministers of Defence are concerned. Then you asked about the commanders. There was General Torbica, the commander of -- he was the commander as of May. Who the corps commander was before that of the JNA, I'm not quite sure, but he was a Serb from Lika. I assume he was born there, his origins were there. Then there was a commander General Milan Celeketic. He was from Western Slavonia. Well, at least, I'm not quite sure but he lived in Western Slavonia. Whether he was actually born there I'm not sure. Then there was General Mile Mrksic, and he was a native of Kordun. I've already said that. Now, whether he was actually born there or whether his antecedents were from Kordun, I'm not sure. What else did you ask me? Was there anything else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we get a collective answer, can you summarise -- would it be right to say that none of them were born outside Krajina? Of all the ones you've mentioned, you seem to have picked your brains and recollected all these individuals. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told you what I know about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine, very well. Let's move on to your other assertions with respect to Kijevo and the fighting that took place in 1991. Why do you say that in the struggles and battles around Kijevo and for Kijevo, units of the JNA were engaged when you personally, you yourself in your statement - I don't want to go back into private session so I won't quote the exact date the paper this appeared in and all the rest - but you said that no forces whatsoever from Yugoslavia took part in the fighting to liberate Kijevo, Vrlika, and so on, and some other things as well which I don't want to mention because I would prefer to stay in open session.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I knew. Now, in the context I did that, I cannot repeat here and now, but I said what I knew, and I have told this Tribunal what I know, and I can repeat that. So in the battles for Kijevo, to the best of my knowledge, the Knin Corps of the JNA took part with the use of the artillery and infantry as well as the participation of a separate brigade commanded by Colonel Djukic. The units were also commanded by the Chief of Staff General Mladic. At that time, the commander of the staff was Spiro Nikolic. What his command role was I assume down the chain of command, but he did have a command function. So we're talking about the JNA. What did you ask me? What was your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's not waste time. I didn't ask you who at the time when this was going on was the commander and Chief of Staff and all the rest of it. All that is written down in the documents. I'm asking you why you're saying that units of the JNA took part in that fighting when you made quite the opposite statement at one point, that you said that it was not true that they had taken part. That's what you said previously.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I might have misspoken. I might have made a slip of the tongue, but I didn't say something I didn't think. I -- the JNA units did participate. The 9th Knin Corps did participate, and I know the commanders that took part in the fighting; General Mladic and Colonel Djukic. I personally saw the units of the corps deployed in the area and I personally saw the commanders the following day, after the battles had been concluded after Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment; there's an objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think when the witness is -- said -- is pointed out to contradiction with a former statement, it should be put to him properly. He should be given a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. We were waiting to go into private session in due course. We don't want to go on going in and out. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, you can refer to this document before we adjourn today or when we come back on Friday. You can refer to the document you're relying on to say that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll go back to the document in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to deprive myself of asking the remaining questions that I have for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that this place, this place Kijevo, is ten or 11 kilometres to the east of Knin along the Knin-Vrlika-Slunj road, and in March 1991, were there forces of the MUP of Croatia in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is along the Knin -- it's not along the Knin-Vrlika-Slunj road, it's along the Knin-Vrlika-Sinj road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Sinj, I made a slip of the tongue and said Slunj instead of Sinj. Yes, and in Kijevo, in that month of March, were the MUP forces of Croatia present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police station was set up, I believe, in April 1991, perhaps in March, the MUP station. I think it was March or perhaps April 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, up until that time, the inhabitants of Kijevo, mostly Croats - that is not in dispute - did they in any way -- were they in any way jeopardised by the Serbs, threatened by the Serbs who lived in the surrounding parts? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also true that in Kijevo and -- the HDZ organisation was functioning, was operational, and that this served the Croatian authorities a purpose, that is to say at all costs they provoked some sort of inter-ethnic clash there although the Serbs did not jeopardise in any way whatsoever, as you said a moment ago, the Croat inhabitants of Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constituency of Kijevo had its deputy, its MP in the Knin Municipal Assembly, and he was a member of the HDZ party. I think his name was Mate Maloca. I might be wrong there but Mate was his first name. So as they had an MP, a deputy in the Municipal Assembly of Knin to represent the HDZ, the HDZ took part in the elections in April and May for the Municipal Assembly seats, I therefore assume on that basis and conclude that they did have an HDZ organisation in Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. And in the first half of 1991, is it true that it was precisely this isolated, shall we say, village, without any great importance, happened to be visited by members of the Main Board and government, Milas and Seks, to call upon the inhabitants of Kijevo to stand up to the authorities in Knin and the Yugoslav People's Army? Is that what happened? Are you aware of that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in the month of March, that is to say when the MUP police station of Croatia was set up, the JNA for the first time in the region of Suvo Polje -- Suho Polje, that is to say around Kijevo, they were there and I know that Seks came to Kijevo by helicopter. I don't know who accompanied him. And they held speeches there, lending their support to the inhabitants of Kijevo and the police station in Kijevo, and the helicopter was shot at from the Serb side, and people even said that it had been hit but that the helicopter managed to pull itself out, to extricate itself from the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said a moment ago that the Serbs who lived in the surrounding parts of Kijevo did not jeopardise the Croats in any way. Now, is it clear, at least from what we have just taken note of, that pressure was brought to bear over the inhabitants of Kijevo to create an incident and to clash with the authorities and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first said that the inhabitants of Kijevo were not jeopardised by the surrounding Serbs who lived in the surrounding parts, but they were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. under jeopardy by a group from Golubic, that is to say a DB and police group from Golubic. And this group already at the end of April and certainly from the beginning of May did some sporadic shooting. There was sporadic shooting from Golubic towards Kijevo and the police station there, or the Kijevo settlement, and in one of these drives a native of Polaca was killed. Vaso Pecer was his name. And that was in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was an inhabitant of Polaca?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaso Pecer. Around the 2nd of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was killed, people rumoured that he was killed by the Croats from Kijevo or, rather, the Croatian policemen from Kijevo. But later I learnt some more details about this incident, and I would rather not speak about the dead, because of his family, but I was told that in fact he had taken part in a group of policemen from Golubic who did this sporadic shooting from the Kozjak positions, that is to say from the slopes of Mount Kozjak towards targeting the village of Kijevo and that is in fact how he lost his life, how he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was killed that way, was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was never established who actually killed him. There was this shooting, Kijevo was being targeted, and there was shooting back from Kijevo, so he was killed in this crossfire. But it was never ascertained as to who killed him. There was speculations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. So you say he killed himself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say he killed himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This place Polaca, is that the same place where the Ustashas from Kijevo in 1941 in just one night killed several dozen Serbs? Is that the same Polaca place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to go into that because the time has come up, but what the relevance of that can have for events 50 years later, I don't understand. Now, we'll adjourn -- we will adjourn now, and the UN holiday tomorrow means that we can't sit, but we'll sit on Friday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time, Mr. May, do I have left, according to your arithmetic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two hours and a quarter you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then Mr. Tapuskovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, assuming that the accused and Mr. Tapuskovic take the time allotted - and I understand that the accused will and Mr. Tapuskovic has told me he will - that will leave a limited, at most, amount of time for the next witness. As Your Honour knows, I have competing duties in relation to this case on Friday. It may well be that the next witness will not be reached at all, but if time is available for him to be reached, if this is acceptable to the Chamber, I'll make arrangements for one of my colleagues to take him in chief, if that's acceptable to the institution generally, but I think it's a witness of a kind I ought to be available for for cross-examination, for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it's highly unlikely we're going to reach another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
